Now we come to the Interrogatory.

§ 224
She was a good mother to her children.

When the Servant of God withdrew from the world, her son and her daughter were already in boarding school. As long as she could leave the son in the school, the Servant of God kept him there, and I know that he left there already grown, but I do not know the precise years he then had. Adjoining our house at Piacenza there was, and is, another little house which was bought in the name of the children, and in this the son Alessandro lived when he left school, and he was not traveling here and there, and it was also afterward inhabited by the son-in-law and the daughter. This house was joined to ours, our own having to be enlarged, and an internal door of communication was made on the ground floor, and the son kept the key, so that he could enter our house freely; yet he was never seen.

§ 225
Marriage of the daughter and conflicts with the son-in-law.

Of the daughter I said in another session that after a little boarding school the Servant of God took her back with her. But this happened several times, because the Servant of God made every attempt to keep her away. After barely a year Carlotta wanted to return to her mother, and she was compelled to take her back. Then the mother sought another Institute for her, where she stayed another little while, but then, the girl seeking her mother, the latter was compelled to take her back. So it was done for some time, until about her twentieth year, the Servant of God having succeeded also in placing her in the house of the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi, here in Rome, and in a Convent of cloistered nuns, to see whether with God's help the religious vocation might develop in her. All was useless. Her affection for her mother compelled her to seek her mother, and therefore to take refuge with her. Finally when her daughter was about twenty, the occasion presented itself to the Servant of God of marrying her to a Count of Rome, a certain Gaspare, whose surname I do not recall. This Gentleman was presented to the Servant of God, as she told me, by a priest. The Servant of God telling me one day that the husband made her daughter suffer, I said to her: «But why, mother, did you give her your daughter in marriage?». And she: «You are right, but what do you want? A priest came to present him to me and spoke so well of him, assuring me that he would treat my daughter very well; on the other hand, she absolutely wanted to take a husband, threatening otherwise to throw herself from the window. I no longer knew what to do, and persuaded that the priest's words were truthful, I did not think of money, and contented myself with the persuasion that he would treat her well». It must also be noted that while the daughter was in an Institute for the deaf-mute, her mother was compelled to remove her from there because she learned that she had fallen in love with a deaf-mute man. Adjoining this generalate house in Rome, a little villa was built, of which one floor belonged to the daughter, one to the son, and a third to the brother Federico. Here, however, there was no internal communication. The son-in-law nevertheless kept the key to the gate of our house, so that he could enter whenever he wished. The portresses, however, were warned by the Servant of God that when someone from there (that is, of her relatives) entered, they should warn her by a special sign of the little bell; and regarding the possibility of dangers, I repeat what I have already said about the house at Piacenza. I know that these relatives saw me unwillingly, I being always present at their conversations with the mother, as she herself wished. Only sometimes, notwithstanding the mother's wish, I absented myself during some conversation with the mother; and I am persuaded that, so that no danger should arise with the relatives for her Religious, she used more than sufficient precautions.

§ 226
Fortitude in facing the demands of the family.

Proc. fol. 489: Once, when the Servant of God was on summer holiday near Fiesole, in a villa near which another little villa was situated, on the day of St. Rose, Nonni, who had come to celebrate her grandmother's name day, said to her: «Today, grandmother, you must pay for my feast, and you should buy me that little villa situated near here», and she insisted on this request. But the Servant of God, after repeatedly refusing her, concluded: «You say what you like, but the little villa I cannot buy for you and I shall not buy it. I have no money, and I would not even have come here on holiday if the money for this purpose had not been given me as a gift. How do you want me to be able to make you such gifts? You would make me go to the Holy Office». On the day of St. Rose these relatives of hers did not fail to come and pester the Servant of God, although she showed that she cared little for them, and sometimes even reproved them. (The Sisters, however, in this case intervened, excusing the relatives and saying to the Servant of God: «Let it be, Mother, they did well to come».) These relatives, now one now another, came almost every day to the Servant of God, although most of the time she, as I said above, showed she cared little for them, and even reproved them.

Once the Servant of God gave Nonni a harp as a gift, handing the money to her father so that he might send it to the maker. But the maker, after a certain time, not seeing the money, which Nonni's father had pocketed, claimed it from the Servant of God, who was thus compelled to pay out another three thousand lire. At this fact the Servant of God was a little upset, reproved the son-in-law and declared to his wife that from then on she would no longer tolerate the son-in-law in her presence. And whereas before the Servant of God also entrusted commissions to him, for example to go and collect money that came to her from America, she no longer entrusted any charge to him, no longer trusting him. And from that time the son-in-law was seen rarely in the house. In the first times the son-in-law was esteemed good by the Sisters. Almost every morning he made Communion, almost every morning he came to the Chapel to serve Mass, all things which led the Sisters to the said favorable judgment. I too, in the first times when I was with the Servant of God, having a good opinion of him, said to her: «Mother, Gaspare is good, you know», and I said this to her because I saw her little favorable toward him. But the Servant of God answered me: «My daughter, you do not know him yet, you will learn to know him, he is not sincere». I do not know whether what I am about to relate happened before or after the fact of the harp, because both this and the preceding fact I heard narrated by the Servant of God and by Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi, I not yet being resident in Rome when they happened. Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi, when she was Superior of the house at Florence, once had six thousand lire given her by a Lady, for having been cared for by our Sisters; and she intended to send it to the Servant of God. It happened, however, that in those days the son-in-law of the Servant of God passed through; she thought well to hand it to him to bring to the mother, writing at the same time to the mother that she was seizing this occasion, which seemed to her more convenient, for the transmission of that money. But that money never reached its destination. It is to be noted that Solenghi had handed the letter for the Servant of God to her son-in-law and therefore never received a single line of answer, nor of receipt. Having then come to Rome after a certain time, it became clear that the son-in-law had kept the money for himself, denying even to his mother-in-law that he had received anything from Solenghi. Since this son-in-law went around the houses, and could have pocketed other money, the Servant of God sent a Circular to her houses recommending that nothing be handed to her son-in-law.

§ 227
Serene attitude of the Servant of God in the Apostolic Visitation.

Ad 25: I know of one Apostolic visitation only. Mons. Cavicchioni, later Cardinal, since our Cardinal Protector was Alimonda, Archbishop of Turin, was deputed to represent him at this generalate house; for this I saw him come several times to the Servant of God and deal with her, but I do not know who was ever Apostolic Visitor. A year before the Apostolic Visitor was named and began his office, the Servant of God, in her familiar conversations with me (no one in this house knowing anything of it), told me that a visitation ordered by the Vatican would come; and my asking her how she knew this, she answered me that she saw a sign from time to time, and at times, even while speaking with me, by which she understood that the said visitation was to come. She saw, she told me further, especially when she prayed, a geographical map of the Institute, that is, a map in which were marked the cities where the houses of the Institute were, and as it were a mitre that was carried from this to that house. And my asking her further: «Why ever this visitation?». She answered me: «It is seen that they will not be pleased with the Institute». And my replying what she would do with this visitation, she added: «The visitor, if he finds good, will write good; if he finds evil, will write evil». Turning at times to the Lord, she said to him: «If so you will, O my Lord, may your will be done. If you will it, it will be for the good of the Institute». I telling her further that she was mistaken: «Let us hope it is not so». With all assurance she replied that so it would be. She was nevertheless calm of spirit before this prophetic vision of hers. I asked the Servant of God further to pray the Lord to let her know the cause of this visitation, and who had provoked it, because, as I saw it, someone must have been there who had reported ill of the Institute to the Holy See. The Servant of God, however, refused to pray for this purpose, pointing out to me that it could not please the Lord that she ask him to reveal to her the author of accusations against the Institute, and she remained firm in this refusal, although I replied that it did not seem to me wrong to ask this of the Lord.

§ 228
She had knowledge of the Apostolic Visitation through supernatural lights.

Proc. fol. 504v.: Not only did the Servant of God have previous knowledge, by supernatural light, of the future Apostolic Visitation, but the Lord also communicated to her the knowledge of the various places, here and there, where the Visitor was on the occasion of his visitation. It is indeed true that when the Visitor undertook the Visitation of some region where the Institute has houses, he came to the Servant of God to warn her that he would undertake the visitation of such and such a region, but did not tell her the order he would follow, as I learned from the Servant of God herself. The Servant of God then gave him the money she presumed needed for the journey, adding that if he needed more, he should let her know. When afterward the Visitor was in a region, the Servant of God told me: «Today the Visitor is in that house»; then, some other day, she told me: «Today he is in that other». And my asking how the Servant of God knew, she either did not answer me at all, or sometimes told me: «The Lord has let me know». And my replying: «Mother, when did he let you know? While I am present or else in the Chapel, or elsewhere?». And she then did not answer.

§ 229
She cooperated humbly with the Visitor.

When she did not answer my request, how she knew, then I asked the Secretary and the others of the council whether and when she had received letters from the Visitor or from the Sisters of the Region where the Visitor was. And their answering me that for so many days she had received no letter from that quarter, I was convinced that the Servant of God had received news of the houses by supernatural gift, those times when she had not wished to answer me. Sometimes, however, she knew it by ordinary ways, and she then told me. When the Visitor gave the Servant of God advance notice that he would begin the Visitation in such a Region, the Servant of God in turn gave advance notice to the various Superiors, commanding them to hide nothing from the Visitor, to be most sincere and to say all they knew of good and evil, and threatened with punishments those who refused to present themselves to the Visitor. I sought the reasons for this Apostolic visitation some time after it had begun, and learned from Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and from Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza that this visitation had been caused by appeals made to the Holy See by some Sisters and by Count Barbiellini, son-in-law of the Servant of God. In these appeals they would have asserted that the affairs of the Institute were not going well, that the Servant of God made her Sisters suffer, and especially the sick, through lack of necessities, to favor her relatives. I then heard, by chance, in that year in which I was with the Servant of God on holiday at the Squerzoni (of which I have already spoken another time), a conversation on this matter between Count Barbiellini Gaspare and his eldest daughter nicknamed «Nonni», held under some trees near the window of my room, from which I saw and heard without being seen.

§ 230
The son-in-law of the Servant of God and the Apostolic visitation.

It was of this tenor. The Count told his daughter that he himself had worked to bring the Apostolic visitation to our Institute, which had already begun; that he himself had induced the Sisters Anna Amabile (now of the house in America, but then provincial of Naples) and Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi (now, I believe, of the house in France) (and I do not recall whether he added other names, and I understand that these revealed names are not to be made public, even after the publication of the present process, since they could cause harm to the same) to write, as he had done, to the Holy Congregation; that Mons. Serafini would certainly do as he told him, because he had been his friend for a long time, having known him since he was in school; now, he added, Mons. Serafini will make the visitation to the house of Rome, there he will naturally find, as I told him, that things are not going well and will make the Superior General resign, and the Institute will be dissolved. And if the Institute is successfully dissolved, all the property of the Institute is ours, because the grandmother is ours. And Nonni added: «And I want my share, and we shall settle accounts with Mons. Serafini». When I heard this conversation, a certain Sr. Anna Borromea, who acted as cook, now deceased, was in the room with me, but still in bed because it was very early in the morning, and so heard only a murmur of words, without perceiving them, all the more since the conversation was in a low voice; and for this she asked me what they were saying, but I thought well to tell her nothing else than that they intended to settle accounts with Mons. Serafini when they returned to Rome, and I did not report this conversation even to the Servant of God, after, however, having taken counsel with the Confessor, who said to me: «Let them chatter, they have always chattered and will always chatter, therefore say nothing».

§ 231
Docile and deferential toward the Visitor.

I note the coincidence of the Count's words with the fact that at that time the Servant of God was governing the Institute almost as provisional, the Visitor having told her at the beginning of August: «You will govern the Institute until November, when you have returned to Rome, and then we shall think what we should do». And since I must narrate the Apostolic Visitation, I shall say that the said words which I reported above were said to the Visitor in the first visit he made to the Servant of God; that she showed herself docile and most deferential to the Visitor; that she submitted with all docility to the order the Visitor gave her, not to open new houses without his permission during this provisional nature of government; that the Servant of God not only accepted these limitations well, but offered the Visitor also her resignation on the spot, if he saw that she was not fit to govern the Institute well, but that the Visitor did not accept this offer. Of this conversation I had news from the Servant of God herself and from Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega. I recall this particular, told me by Sr. Anna Benedetta: that the Servant of God showed herself tranquil and serene in all the time of the said visitation of Mons. Serafini, that when he took leave, she accompanied him graciously to the door and then said to her sisters: «Now leave me in peace, for I need to retire to my room for some hours». As in fact she retired and was not seen until the following morning to hear Holy Mass. When she came out she was seen of very suffering appearance, but, asked whether she felt ill, answered she felt well, and throughout the day showed herself serene and tranquil. As I heard from various Sister Superiors, who had come to the Servant of God, she had recommended to them to answer with sincerity all the Visitor's questions and to let him see everything; in a particular way, then, she recommended showing him the pantry, the cupboards, and that nothing, in short, be hidden from him.

Sometimes, having asked the Servant of God whether this visitation would turn out well, she answered me: «This visitation is ordered by authority, and therefore it cannot turn out other than for the good of the Institute».

§ 232
Trust in God during the Apostolic Visitation.

At other times, having expressed to her my doubt, rather my persuasion, that such a visitation would not turn out for the good of the Institute and that in this visitation little trust was shown in her, she answered me: «Jesus wills it, and how can it turn out to harm if Jesus wills it? and if little trust is shown in me, what does it matter? St. Teresa too underwent an Apostolic Visitation, and what harm did she have from it? So for me». I was never questioned by the Visitor, although I would have been glad of it. This happened because when the Visitor went to Piacenza I was in Rome, and when the Visitor came to Rome I was by chance at Piacenza. This Apostolic visitation lasted about five years, that is, until the General Chapter after the death of the Servant of God to elect her Successor. The Visitor always showed himself deferential toward the Servant of God; he came to visit her twice during her last illness; another time after she had already received Extreme Unction, and he pontificated the Requiem Mass on the seventh day after her death. I shall even add that he had come another time to visit her, and the Servant of God had already expired.

§ 233
From youth she always observed the divine commandments.

Ad 26: From what I know directly, the Servant of God observed faithfully and scrupulously the commandments of God and of the Church; and from what I was able to learn from her brothers, especially from Federico, also from girlhood, and then from what I have heard said by the other Sisters, she always observed them scrupulously. The Servant of God speaking to me confidentially, told me very well of her late husband, and other things from which it was easy to understand how she was wholly submissive to him and cared for him. From her mouth too I learned how much care and concern she had for the soul and the body of her children. In short, I hold as most certain that the Servant of God always observed with great fidelity the duties of her various states.

Ad 27: There is no doubt for me that the Servant of God practiced all the virtues, Theological and Cardinal, humility, obedience, poverty.

§ 234
Heroic faith of the Servant of God.

Faith: I never doubted that the Servant of God always believed all the truths revealed by the Church. And I myself heard her exclaim: «O my God, rather than fail in a single point of your faith, let me die». At times when I was with the Servant of God and we were both silent, I heard that the Servant of God interrupted it to drive away some temptation against faith, saying: «Lord, I am tempted against faith, but I believe, and even if the devil threw me into the fire, I shall never fail in my faith in you. In whatever place I may be thrown, you will always come to my aid».

When I heard these exclamations, I kept silent, because I saw the Servant of God wholly absorbed. Sometimes, when the Servant of God broke out into the above-mentioned expressions, I heard a great noise of glass and din in her room; a din such that it was impossible to confuse it with an earthquake; a noise of chains, of wood falling, and the Servant of God then asked me: «Are you afraid?». I answered no; but had she not been there, who knows where I would have fled. These noises I heard by day and also by night, when, in the last times of the Servant of God, I did not leave her at night; at a very late hour, that is, about midnight, I slept in an adjoining room. These noises were also heard by other Sisters, as I know from the questions they asked me the next morning to learn what had happened, and I answered them: «What do I know?». Because the mother did not want these things to be known by others.

§ 235
Apostolate of catechesis from motives of faith.

Proc. fol. 529v.: Already from when the Servant of God was a girl she busied herself with the Catechism, and as a Daughter of Mary went to teach it in the Churches. She resumed this apostolate as a widow, and when she was a religious she always recommended it to her Sisters. I recall that she often went to the Novitiate to question the Novices (and as long as she felt well she did so every Sunday) to see whether they were sufficiently instructed in the catechism to be able to teach it to others. She gave them conferences on the subject, encouraging them in this apostolate. When she then visited the houses, one of the first things to which she exhorted her Sisters was the catechetical instruction of children. She herself sometimes went to give catechism in the Churches.

She then wanted her Sisters to do as much for adults; and one day, my observing to the Servant of God that adults did not need catechism, she answered me: «Sometimes they need it more than the little ones». With true joy of her soul, she sent her daughters to America and to Africa, and wherever there was good to be done to souls, to convert those who err, and all who are outside our Church.

§ 236
In the visitations she watched over prayer.

Proc. fol. 537: The first thing the Servant of God concerned herself with, in her visit to the houses, was this: whether people prayed, not only keeping to the rules, but whether they abounded in prayers, especially to Jesus in the Sacrament, whom she did not want ever left alone, but visited frequently by one Sister or another, or by the school girls. She also suggested that sometimes, as opportunity allowed, outsiders too be led into the chapel, to say a little prayer to Jesus in the Sacrament. She required that in the houses daily Mass never be lacking, and desired sacramental Communion likewise daily.

Sr. Camilla Valentini told me that once, when the Servant of God was making her visit to a house, she first went, as usual, to make a visit to Jesus in the Sacrament in the Chapel, which had been adorned, and all the lights had been lit in it. The Servant of God, after remaining on her knees about a quarter of an hour, turning, called the Superior and said to her: «How is it that you do not have Jesus in the Sacrament?». The Superior was surprised and mortified, because the fact was true, and she believed the Foundress knew nothing, as indeed no one had told her. Then, having left the Chapel, she reproved her and wanted it provided for immediately: «For, she said, if Jesus is lacking, life is lacking to the Religious».

§ 237
She prayed continually: she seemed an angel.

When the Servant of God prayed, her face composed itself in such a way, and her whole person, that she seemed an angel. She did not answer anyone who called her, especially in the prayers before and after Mass and during meditation. In the Chapel she was accustomed to kneel at a prie-dieu; but after Communion she remained on her knees always on the bare floor, leaning on a chair, for the space of an hour, and this always when she went to the Chapel, even when ill in the last times.

The prayer of the Servant of God, as I have said, was, one may say, continual; she prayed in the Chapel and she prayed in her own room by day and by night. Often she prayed in her own room, called me to keep her company, and we prayed together; but frequently our prayer was interrupted, she remaining as if absorbed, and I, after waiting some time to see whether she returned to herself, when I saw that this kind of ecstasy continued, quietly, quietly, went out.

§ 238
In anxieties she had recourse to the Crucifix.

Proc. fol. 552: In anxieties and tribulations the Servant of God always had recourse to the Crucifix, and sought to instill this devotion in her Religious as well. She loved the Cross and told us, her Religious, that if we did not love the Cross we would not be spouses of Jesus Christ. When the Superiors of other houses came to her complaining of the Crosses they had to bear in government, the Servant of God, taking the Crucifix in her hand and showing it to the one who complained, said: «Then you do not love the Crucifix; if you loved him you would not complain; the Cross is our way». And she then continued to comfort her with the example of Jesus Crucified and added: «What we suffer is nothing; come, courage». If someone complained of the character of some religious, she said: «Jesus bears with us all, and shall we, for love of him, refuse to bear with one another?». This I heard from many Superiors. To the sick she then said: «Oh! well, Jesus makes you share in his Cross; carry it willingly». And this I learned from the sick many times. Every day the Servant of God recited the chaplet of our Lord, consisting of thirty-three Our Fathers and thirty-three little prayers, as in our community prayer book. Then every day she likewise recited the little chaplet of the Immaculate. And these two chaplets she wanted prescribed to her religious too. She, however, in particular, added other prayers to Jesus Crucified, to the Most Precious Blood, to the five wounds. Every year on the evening of Holy Thursday, after the Rosary she withdrew to her room, not to leave it until seven or eight o'clock on Holy Saturday. In that time she did not open or answer anyone, except on the evening of Good Friday, and then she opened, when necessary, to receive a dish of boiled greens, and nothing else, and closed again immediately.

§ 239
Eucharistic life.

Proc. fol. 564: Most devoted to the Eucharist, every day, without fail, she received Communion, and as far as I know she never omitted it on any day. She herself told me that even as a lay person she had never omitted daily Communion. She spared no sacrifice in order to be able to receive Communion. If necessary she stopped at some place, before reaching the end of her journey, for the purpose of receiving Communion. She warned by letters or telegrams the houses where she was to arrive, so that a Priest would be provided for her to receive Communion. The last journey she made was from Genoa to Rome, and she was in such poor health that she made it accompanied by the priest and the doctor, and arriving here she received Communion. She had the privilege, in the last time of her life (I do not know whether six months or a year), of being able to take something before communicating, but she almost never made use of it, preferring to have the Priest come a little after midnight rather than avail herself of the privilege obtained. She was scrupulous, however, in this too: therefore only for a few nights when she returned from Genoa in poor health, as I said before, in the month of September 1899 she had the Priest come immediately after midnight, and as soon as she felt better she no longer inconvenienced him, and returned to receiving Communion immediately after midnight, when she again grew worse, that is, about a month before dying. I recall that the doctor had forbidden her in the last times to get out of bed early, therefore she provided herself with permission to receive Communion in bed immediately after midnight.

Proc. fol. 569: Sometimes in the last times of her life, and sometimes also by reason of travel, she could not hear Mass; but at times it was celebrated for her in the room adjoining her bedroom, so that she could hear it without too much inconvenience, and she, those times, rose from bed and took those few steps to go to the other room to hear Mass. This happened few times and especially on Sundays. Long and most diligent was the Servant of God's preparation for Holy Communion, and the thanksgiving lasted at least an hour. When she received Communion immediately after midnight, after receiving the Sacred Particle, she signaled me to go away, and I returned at four in the morning, and even then I found her in prayer. Strange was the surprise the Servant of God showed me most often when I presented myself to her again, as I said, at four in the morning. «Oh! you are here already, — she said to me, — did you not go to rest?» and I: «Yes, mother, I went and now it is already four». And she: «It seemed to me you had gone out just now». And I: «But who knows what you do after Communion? Sometimes I want to stay behind the door to hear». And she: «You are a great little tarocchina» (a word meaning chatterbox).

§ 240
She promoted daily communion and first communions. § 241
She also promoted spiritual communions.

She exhorted her Sisters to receive Communion daily whenever the occasion arose, and especially in her visit to the houses, and I myself heard her say to them: «A Sister who does not receive Jesus has nothing in herself». When some Religious came from outside and arrived before eleven in the morning, she asked them whether they were still fasting and whether they were disposed to make Communion, and exhorted them to make it if the Confessor was still at the house at that hour, and more than once she sent me to see whether he was there.

To promote first Communion also among children, she also established in our Church the Congregation of the Luigini. For their eucharistic instruction, these were gathered by the Sisters in the Sacristy, where a priest then came for their Catechism. She concerned herself with the frequent Communion of the sick Sisters, and for the sick at home, in whose assistance the Sisters engaged, she exhorted them saying: «Take good care that they receive the Sacraments», and suggested to them all the means for succeeding in the intent even in difficult cases, such as when the family would not permit, or the sick person had difficulty from fear of death or human respect.

She also took care that her Religious made frequent spiritual communions. She said to the Novices: «You made few, but you will have made them well, is it not so? tomorrow you will make a few more, and always well». She suggested to them the most fitting way to make Spiritual Communion and the thoughts useful for it. For example she said to them: «We here at home always revolve around Jesus in the Sacrament; if we go by the stairs we have nearby the chapel where Jesus is in the Tabernacle; if we go to the terrace to walk or hang out the laundry or do other work, near us are the windows of the church where Jesus is in the Sacrament. Everything, in short, invites us to unite ourselves to him, and urges us to Spiritual Communion. Everything in the house recalls us to Jesus, and we should be like the Seraphim of love. And how could we not unite ourselves to Him spiritually?». The affairs of the Institute the Servant of God attended to especially in the morning after Holy Mass, and she wrote the letters she did not think proper to entrust to others (to the Superiors in America she always wrote herself), and in writing she was extremely quick, so that she seemed a little machine. The rest of the day, except when she was occupied with strictly necessary and urgent things and was not obliged to listen to Sisters come from elsewhere, she spent more than anything in the Chapel near Jesus, and a little withdrawing to her room.

§ 242
She celebrated the feast of Corpus Christi with great solemnity.

Proc. fol. 578: She wanted in all her houses the feast of Corpus Christi to be celebrated with the greatest solemnity possible. I recall that at the feast of 1897 or 98, the Servant of God having entered the Church shortly before the Procession began, she herself opened the gates of the Church and had the Procession file out into the street, to then bring it back in by the door of the house. To the remark of her brother Francesco that they might fine her for some contravention, she replied: «Leave me be, you will see nothing happens». Curious were the remarks of the people who were watching our Procession, on seeing all of us dressed for the feast, and the Servant of God, as usual, in a colored and frayed apron. «That poor old woman, — they said — nobody looks at her, nobody cares for her; she is so poorly dressed, while the others are dressed for the feast, they have not even given her the candle, while the others all have it». I recall that she was told: «Mother, you do not have a candle». And she: «Let us hope my heart serves as a candle». I recall that on that occasion even the tram stopped, although we did not occupy its rails. I also recall that on that occasion she wanted the whole house decked with flags, in the corridors where the Most Blessed Sacrament passed she wanted to see vases of flowers, and that many children dressed as little angels follow the Procession.

One morning, while I was in the Sacristy of this our Church (it happened perhaps in the fourth year that I was with the Servant of God), she came down into the Church and came to look for me in the Sacristy, saying to me: «Come, Sr. Anna Serafina, let us go and pray to the Sacred Heart». After ten minutes she asked me for a chair to climb onto the altar, but I, for greater safety, brought her a little stepladder, and climbed up myself to remove the candlesticks and open the little door before the statue. I having come down, the Servant of God went up, knelt on the step of the altar table, then asked me for a cloth, which I thought she wanted to dust the statue of the Sacred Heart. And therefore I offered to climb up myself to dust; but she said to me: «I will do it». The cloth I handed her she put aside, and taking her white handkerchief from her pocket she stood up and began to wipe the hands and forehead of the statue, which, as I saw and contemplated at length, were emitting blood from the wounds; and the blood that came from the hands was very copious. It also emitted blood from the Heart, and the Servant of God dried that blood too. I did not see the blood come from the wounds of the feet, because the Servant of God prevented it with her person. I note that at that time there was not the tabernacle that is on the altar today. The Servant of God remained at this operation about an hour; I was amazed at this sight and said to myself: «What mystery is this?». Then I said to the Mother: «What is the matter with the Sacred Heart? does he feel ill?». But the Servant of God did not answer me. At my second insistence she answered me only: «Pray, pray». And she and I prayed each on our own. After about an hour, as I said, I no longer saw the blood flow from the wounds of the Sacred Heart.

§ 243
Ardent devotion to Our Lady.

Proc. fol. 587: Returning to speak of the devotion of the Servant of God to Our Lady, I shall say that she prescribed to her Institute, besides the daily Rosary, the Little Chaplet of the Immaculate and that of the Sorrowful Mother; she added to this, though I could not assure whether every day, the office of Our Lady. On Saturdays for this devotion she had Eucharistic Benediction given in the public Church and in the Chapel adjoining here. She was so devoted to the Immaculate of Lourdes that she was not content until she found the benefactor soul who would make for her in our public Church a facsimile of the grotto of Lourdes. She also wanted Our Lady of Lourdes in all her houses, where possible, and in those houses that lacked sufficient means she provided for them directly. I was at Prato when the Servant of God sent from France to that house a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes, to be placed in the Chapel of that House. So that the facsimile of the grotto of Lourdes in this our Church on Via Merulana might turn out as similar as possible, she herself went on pilgrimage to that Shrine in France.

§ 244
Devotion to St. Anne, characteristic of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 604: That the Servant of God was most devoted to St. Anne there is no need to say. The very name given to her Institute attests it, the prayers and practices prescribed to the Institute by the Servant of God in her honor. From the morning wake-up one begins with homage to St. Anne. The wake-up is made invoking her with an aspiration; every hour throughout the day an aspiration is prescribed. Before and after the meal a prayer to St. Anne is made; there is one to her in the morning prayers; another special one on the 26th of every month; and three other prayers on the last three days of every month; the month of July is wholly consecrated in her honor. In every room there must be the image of St. Anne. Besides these devotions and practices which the Servant of God performed, just like her Religious, it was habitual with her to turn to her, to recommend this or that thing to her. To her she attributed many graces she had received for her religious. To her, in a particular way, she recommended her Religious who went to America: «St. Anne, — she told her Sisters, — is our Foundress, and to her we must always commend ourselves, and she will not abandon us; she will guide us, extricate us from the difficulties from which we would not know how to extricate ourselves; she will free us from dangers».

St. Anne often appeared to the Servant of God, and I myself was present, perhaps some twenty times, at these apparitions. Sometimes the Servant of God asked the Saint to show her (always expressing the condition if it were God's will) how this or that house was going. Then the Saint presented her with a vase, in which at times there were flowers, and at other times as many little plants without flowers as there were Sisters in that house about which the Servant of God asked information. The Servant of God the first time did not understand the meaning, and having asked the Saint, she explained to her that the plants with leaves (which hung down from the rim of the vase) without flowers denoted that there was no observance of the rule in that house; the flowers, on the other hand, signified observance. At other times she presented her with very well flowered vases and added: «Be at peace, for in that house the observance of the Rule is in bloom».

§ 245
Other devotions.

Proc. fol. 656v.: The Servant of God was devoted to St. Francis of Assisi. From girlhood she enrolled in the Franciscan Third Order, and as a lay person wore the tunic of St. Francis as an undergarment; and it continued also afterward, when she was a daughter of St. Anne, until she fell ill and it was impossible for her to wear it. After her death we found two: one frayed and the other in better condition. The first was given her by a Capuchin Lay Brother of Genoa whom they called Fr. Santo, and who is now Venerable. She also composed a prayer to St. Francis and prescribed its recitation to her Institute every day. And in the rules she wrote that we are the minimae of St. Francis, and wanted the linen of the communities to bear the letters: A.M.F., meaning: Anna, Maria, Francesca. She inculcated to the Sisters her example of penance, humility and poverty.

For St. Joachim she composed a prayer which we recite every day.

§ 246
The Cardinal Protector and the Servant of God in a very particular dispute.

Proc. fol. 700: Once the Cardinal Protector Verga desired that a certain Anna Francesca (I do not recall the surname), already assigned to the General Secretariat, be named general Secretary, and asked it of the Servant of God, telling her she would be most suitable for that post, but the Servant of God let him understand that she could not accede to his wish. The Cardinal insisting on his request, and the General Chapter drawing near, and fearing therefore that the Cardinal would exercise his authority in favor of that Sister whom he wanted general secretary, the Servant of God turned to St. Anne and invited me too to pray with her.

As the time of the Chapter then drew near, Sr. Anna Francesca feeling not very well, the Servant of God followed the counsel given her by St. Anne, and so that Sister went to Naples. And this was the incident that made the Cardinal sulk, who began to thin out his visits and to come to us no more. That Sister then stayed some years in Naples. The Servant of God once had Sr. Anna Francesca come from Naples, and she, alighting at the Rome station, instead of coming directly to our house, went first to the Cardinal Protector. I remember well that when Sr. Anna Francesca was here in Rome, if she went out of the house, the Servant of God always had her accompanied by some Sister of her own trust. And I recall that once, the Superior of the Hospital of Naples having come to Rome, who had been in relation with Sr. Anna Francesca, and she wishing to go out with that Superior, the Servant of God did not permit it. When the Cardinal Protector came, and the Servant of God did not have him told that she was busy, and received him, as always, in her study, I stayed there little, while, on the other hand, those assigned to the Secretariat were present, some of the assistants and some of those who had arrived from elsewhere. I heard, however, that the Servant of God made her excuses to the Cardinal because the previous time she had not presented herself to him, being busy. Given the short time I stayed, I could not notice anything special in the demeanor of the Servant of God; she herself, however, told me sometimes that the Sisters had asked her whether she felt ill, because they had seen her a little serious and disturbed, but that she had answered she had nothing. And the Sisters again, like Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, asked me on that occasion whether the Servant of God felt ill, because they had seen her as if preoccupied. When the Cardinal Protector no longer came to this our house, I recall that, the Servant of God and I with her being on holiday at the Villa Pontellini at Fiesole, and having learned that the Cardinal, traveling, would pass through Florence, she hastened to have an invitation reach him for a visit at that villa; but the Cardinal did not come. After this fact, the following November, he passed by this generalate house together with his nephew, a Priest, and stopped, only the nephew however alighting to greet the Servant of God. Learning that His Eminence the Protector was in the carriage below at the gate, she herself went down to invite the Cardinal to deign to enter, and he not wishing to alight, she had the carriage enter the garden, went into the kitchen to take broth and a beaten egg to give the Cardinal, who was already a little poor in health. She did not succeed, however, in making him get down from the carriage. The Cardinal then having fallen ill with his last illness, which was very long, the Servant of God often sent the Sisters to get news, but he never let them through. Then the Servant of God wished to go herself in person, hoping to see him, but she was not allowed through, although the nephew and the other relatives begged him to let her through. The Servant of God offered the assistance of her Sisters, but it was not accepted.

§ 247
Particular prayers to St. Anne during the Apostolic Visitation.

Proc. fol. 707: I recall that when the Servant of God, during the Apostolic visitation, was worried about the reports the Sisters would make to the Visitor, and about what he would find in some house, she turned to St. Anne, and we prayed together, and St. Anne appearing, I remember, almost always told the Servant of God, who asked her, that the Visitor had been favorably impressed. I recall that only sometimes, about some matter, the Servant of God said that the Visitor had not been altogether favorably impressed. It is to be noted, however, that the Servant of God, for those houses in which the Visitor did not receive a happy impression, as for the others, foresaw it well, and before the Visitor set out for those houses, she had informed and forewarned him that there was such and such a house which would not please him, but that she had already thought of providing as soon as she could, either by visiting the house herself, or by sending the Provincial, or in some other way. I recall that the Servant of God also asked St. Anne whether the Visitor had been pleased with the house at Gargatano, and that the Saint answered her that he had found the kitchen, the pantry, the rooms, etc., good, but that it had not pleased him that two Sisters were there under punishment.

I recall further that at the end of the Apostolic Visitation, before the Visitor handed in his mandate, the Servant of God turned to St. Anne to know what, on the whole, was the impression the Apostolic Visitor had carried away. And St. Anne, appearing to her, I being present, answered her that all had gone well. I recall further that in an apparition of St. Anne, I again being present, the Servant of God asked her what report he had left to the superiors about the visitation made to the Institute, and the Saint answered her that the report the Visitor had presented was splendid, to the glory of the Institute.

§ 248
Apparition of the Child Jesus.

I recall that the Servant of God told me that when she, still unmarried, went to assist the sick, the Child Jesus often appeared to her and encouraged her in these works of charity, and accompanied her to the bedside of the sick person, at times also at night. And if the patient was going to die, he warned the Servant of God so that she might procure the Sacraments for him. So too from the Servant of God's talk I understood perfectly that the Child Jesus appeared to her many other times, when she was still unmarried, helping her, encouraging her. However I cannot say many particulars of that time when I was not at her side, because the Servant of God was averse to telling me of it, and only through the continual habit and familiarity I had with her, from her conversation I was able to catch what I know. Naturally I provoked talk about the times when I was not with her and she had been privileged by the Lord, and I tried to make her speak. For example, she alluding to the times of her youth and to some apparition or supernatural communication, exclaimed: «Oh! what beautiful moments those were that I spent!». And I then tried to make her speak and said to her: «Yes, Mother, oh! truly?». And she: «Oh! the Child Jesus once in that place let me hear music»; «Oh! truly, — I said, — who knows what beautiful sounds! What were they like, Mother?» and she: «Oh! no one can imagine». And I: «Was there also the harp? Did they play the harp too? Did they play well? Like Professor Lorenzi?» (I note that we were at that time at the Villa Pontinelli in Fiesole). At this name, Lorenzi, she started, and exclaimed: «But what am I saying? just look, I was lost in thought». I then tried to make her fall back into the topic by speaking of music, because I knew she liked it so much, but there was no longer any way to make her resume the talk, and I recall that she diverted it by speaking to me even of sorb apples. So I could never come to know all the particulars of her heavenly communications of the times when I was not with her, because it is true that I managed to make her speak a little, but she always broke off as soon as she noticed.

Speaking to me one day of the condescension of Jesus in coming eucharistically into our breast, she began to speak of the first times when she received Communion every day (as far as I could gather by asking her the time when she received Communion every day, it went back to the age of 15 or 17) and said to me: «Oh! when I then approached to receive Jesus! I saw him at times in the form of a radiant child, and it confused me to think that he made himself so little to enter into my breast». And I then said to her: «So, Mother, you did not take pleasure in receiving Communion?». And she: «Oh! not at all that, I did it very willingly, but it grieved me to see him first in the Host in natural size, and to think that he would have to shrink to enter my breast; it gave me the impression that he must suffer in adapting himself to the smallness of my breast». This talk was made several times by the Servant of God, and I sometimes said to her: «Oh! who knows what consolations you must have felt in receiving Communion then»; and she: «Oh! yes, sometimes I understood nothing more; I tucked myself into a corner and was aware of nothing, and if they had not come to look for me, I would have stayed there kneeling who knows how long. Sometimes I was sought at noon, and I was still there, having made Communion early in the morning». Returned then home, to the remark the mother made about her having delayed so much, she answered: «Oh! truly I delayed too long, but I had fallen asleep». At this point of the story I tried to learn something more by saying to her: «Asleep indeed! Who knows what beautiful things Jesus must have said to you!». And she: «Oh! how many things you want to know!». And she added nothing more, though I provoked her by telling her that knowing such things served to fervor us too.

Once, speaking to me of prayer, I think I said to her that she was always with Jesus, this thing she did with Jesus, that other Jesus told her, and so it seemed to me that she was on too friendly terms with Jesus, alluding to the apparitions of Jesus she enjoyed. And she replied: «Friendship with Jesus is never enough». «Nevertheless one must sometimes take the mind away from these heavenly matters, otherwise in the things of this world nothing more is accomplished, and yet they must be dealt with». And she added that to take her thought away she had to suffer a little.

At times the Servant of God told me that the Child Jesus, appearing to her, dictated to her what she had to write. This happened when the Servant of God was directress of the Daughters of Mary in Genoa.

The Archbishop of Genoa called the Servant of God one day and said to her: «You must do me this and this»; I do not know precisely what it was, I know however that it was a writing for the Daughters of Mary; perhaps a regulation. The Servant of God answered, alleging her incapacity. But the Archbishop, judging her nonetheless capable, insisted on the task, and the Servant of God obeyed. The Servant of God gave a conference to the Daughters of Mary, telling them that the Archbishop had ordered that writing for them, without saying however that she was the one charged with it. She invited them to pray that things might turn out according to the Archbishop's wish and for their good.

§ 249
Apparition of Our Lady.

Proc. fol. 711v.: At home, then, the Servant of God prayed in her little room, and as she prayed the Immaculate appeared to her and said to her: «Pray, pray, my daughter, for the task given by the Archbishop, and carry it out». And the Servant of God answered Our Lady that she felt incapable. And Our Lady to her: «Dear daughter, do obedience; you did not ask for this task». And the Servant of God: «I shall do obedience, but I would not wish, however, through my incapacity to be the cause of harm to some soul». And Our Lady: «Dear daughter, you will be of harm to no soul». And she vanished. And the Servant of God, after praying some other days still, carried out the task given by the Archbishop, and the writing completed, I do not know whether she sent it or took it personally to the Archbishop, who, having examined the writing, said (this I learned from Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza and from other Sisters whose names I do not now recall): «This I wanted, this I desired», and said other words of praise which I no longer recall.

When the Servant of God was pushed by her parents to marry (which did not at all correspond to her own ideals), she prayed much, and seeing everything dark, as she said, she kept on praying. As I have already related, I having told her one day that she had done wrong to marry, not feeling inclined to that state, she answered me:

§ 250
Married by the will of God; other mystical phenomena.

«You are right», and she added further (what I had not yet said): «I did nothing other than the will of God, because, praying one day to be enlightened, I heard a voice which said to me clearly: "It is God's will that you marry". Then praying before my Crucifix, that very one which would not stay hanging on the Cross, I heard the same thing repeated to me». Regarding this Crucifix I recall having heard from Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and from Sr. Anna Vincenza Tornatore, who is still living and is Superior in a house of southern Italy, that that Crucifix, the first time it spoke to the Servant of God, she was only seven years old.

At other times, always as a widow, she saw in the host, when she received Communion, a great many people in great confusion, but did not know what it meant. The matter communicated to the Confessor, he recommended her to pray, and the next time he would give her the answer. The Servant of God feared that such a vision signified her unworthiness in approaching Holy Communion and would have wished to abstain, but the Confessor ordered her to go on receiving Communion. The Servant of God would have wished to turn to her Crucifix for the desired explanation, but, fearing to do something contrary to the wishes of the Confessor, who had told her to pray, and that he would then give her the answer, she refrained. When afterward she went, the next time, to confession, the Confessor said to her: «I have prayed and I feel inspired to tell you that the Lord wants great things of you and that you should prepare yourself for them». The Servant of God commended herself to her guardian Angel every day, every moment, always; and she often recited, during the day, the Angele Dei. She recommended this devotion to her Sisters; she told them: «From early morning let us commend ourselves to our guardian Angel who must assist us the whole day. Our guardian Angel records all our good actions: let us therefore always stay close to him, who was assigned to us by Jesus from our first birth, and never cause him the slightest displeasure».

§ 251
Most devoted to the souls in purgatory.

Proc. fol. 724v.: The Servant of God was most devoted to the holy souls in Purgatory. She prayed much for them and had others pray. Every day, when she could, the Servant of God recited the seven Penitential Psalms for the souls in Purgatory, and I too, when I could, kept her company. For the same souls she also recited the hundred «requiem». In the Chapel adjoining here she held every Sunday, for the same souls, [the exposition of] the Most Blessed Sacrament after Holy Mass, until noon. To the Novices she prescribed the Miserere, the De Profundis, the Pange lingua, the Veni creator, and the Rosary with the intention of making suffrage for the holy souls in Purgatory.

§ 252
Most devoted to the Pope.

Proc. fol. 764: Unlimited was her devotion toward the Pope, and when she spoke of him she was accustomed to say that he was our God on earth; and she recommended devotion to him to her Sisters, and if these were teachers, she recommended them to instill in their little girls devotion to the Pope. She prayed and had others pray for him every day, saying that no day should be allowed to pass without praying for the Pope, and she recommended to the Superiors not to let the year pass without sending him their offering, because he too had so many expenses to bear for the Church. She also told her Sisters and the Superiors to make outsiders know their duty of giving the offering to the Pope. When she heard from people of the world speaking ill, or the Pope being treated ill, I heard her grieve at it, and I observed the Servant of God turn pale at the account of some fact against the Church.

When Pius IX died she felt a great void and could not find peace, because a great help had been taken from her. She did not allow any Sister to go to the Cemetery without having made a visit to the tomb of Pius IX and commended our Institute to him.

§ 253
She greatly respected the cardinals and the bishops.

Most respectful was the Servant of God toward the Cardinals and the Bishops. And when she knew that one of these was coming as a guest to our house, she turned the whole house upside down. She was most glad to host them, and once, I remember, our house was full of Cardinals and Bishops. It seems to me that there was the Cardinal of Turin, Alimonda, Protector of the Institute, the Archbishop of Naples, the Patriarch of Venice and others, whom I do not recall, with their Secretaries, in all some twenty among Bishops and Cardinals. And this happened in a jubilee of the Holy Father, Leo the Thirteenth.

She prayed and wanted the Sisters to pray every day for the Cardinal Protector. She respected any order that came from him or from the Holy Congregation and carried it out. In opening new houses she did not permit herself to do anything without the consent of the Bishops. When the Bishops opposed the opening of houses, she turned to prayer. She was also most respectful toward all Ecclesiastics.

§ 254
Zeal for the house of God.

Proc. fol. 770v.: The Servant of God was wholly for the house of God. «For God, — she used to say, — nothing is ever enough», therefore she wanted the most beautiful vestments, and in this sacristy of our Church the most beautiful and richest vestments are those of her time. She always wanted the linen beautiful and spotless, and woe if she saw the altar cloth with some stain of wax, wine, or anything else. And once, having drawn near to see a cloth, which she did frequently, and finding it stained with a little wax, she took it away without more and carried it to the laundry, and said to me: «I am afraid you will put it back, and so I took it away». In the sacristy she always appeared unexpectedly, and seeing a lace that I had just then removed from the high altar and set aside, intending to fold it afterward, the Servant of God carried it off, saying I did not know how to keep the things of the Church, and did not give it back to me again and used it for the Chapel adjoining this hall. In a word, she looked at and examined all the linen. When she went to the other houses, she also observed there minutely everything that belonged to the Chapel. She was not content to look at the first cloth, but also the under-cloths. Therefore when it was known in the houses that the Mother was to arrive, everything was done to have the things of the Chapel found in perfect order. She said that if the things of the Chapel as well as of the Community were not kept well, one failed against the vow of poverty.

She wanted the oil used for the lamp of the Most Blessed Sacrament to be good, and used to say: «To me give whatever oil you like, but for Jesus let it be good». She required that the Sisters be in Church with the greatest devotion and the greatest respect, and that when they passed before the Most Blessed Sacrament they make devoutly the genuflection down to the ground, saying that for two reasons one must behave well in Church and make the genuflection well: first, because Jesus is there; second, because we are religious.

The Servant of God absolutely did not want to see dust in the Church, and to satisfy her sometimes it was not enough to remove the dust only once in the day. Woe then if she saw stains on the floor. And if from the little choir she happened to see any, she immediately sent some sister to warn me. When this Church of St. Anne was opened, the other Sisters wanted the candlesticks of the altars to be bought of wood, but she wanted them of metal. The chasubles she wanted all of silk, saying that of other cloth they were rags. This for our Church of St. Anne. For the other Churches or Chapels of the Institute she wanted that, if chasubles of silk could not be had, they should nevertheless be most decent. She wanted the chalices very beautiful and the ciboria too. The Servant of God did everything first for the glory of God, and then to attain Paradise, and this she preached to her Religious, to whom she then added that we religious must not be content to attain Paradise; but that we have the obligation of being great souls before God.

§ 255
She often spoke of paradise. Detachment from the things of the world.

Hope: She often spoke of Paradise and desired it, and awaited it through the merits of Jesus Christ, and said: «By our own merits we shall certainly not arrive there». Yet she did not want our soul to be attached chiefly to Paradise, but to the love of Jesus, and said to us, her daughters: «We religious must try to love Jesus much and ever more, not because he gives us paradise, but he will certainly give it to us if we love him». She did not want, in short, an interested love toward Jesus, but a generous love, and she brought us the example of St. Teresa, of whom she told that, met one day by her Sisters with a bucket of water in one hand and a lighted torch in the other, and asked what she was going to do, she answered: «With this water I am going to put out hell and with this torch to burn paradise», meaning by this that she did not want paradise and hell to exist before the eyes of her nuns as a motive for doing good and avoiding evil, but only Jesus infinitely lovable. She never placed her heart in the things of this world. She felt a most lively repugnance for money, and it was a great sacrifice for her, as she told me, to handle it, and so as not to handle it she did not keep it, she wanted me to keep it. She therefore spoke the truth when she asserted she had no money (and this she happened to say especially to relatives) and likewise spoke the truth when she said that she always had enough money and did not know what to do with it. As for wealth, she never respected persons, and her affection for the Princess of Fitalia had no motive in the latter's wealth. She said that Jesus had never let her lack the necessary money. She never sought comforts and said: «We must not seek to be well, but rather to be ill». Expecting everything from God, she did not become alarmed or agitated. In every kind of tribulation she never lost heart, having all her trust in God, saying: «It is he who inspires people of this world to come to our aid. When it seems to us that our affairs go badly, we must then go and thank the Lord, for since God so wills, we too must be content».

§ 256
Extreme trust in God.

Sometimes she said: «When our affairs turn to the bad, we must be content and thank the Lord, because by this he wishes to test our faith, and then he will come to our aid. The saints were content when things went badly for them, and so we must do too». To her sisters she tried to instill trust and hope in God, and also to every kind of troubled and afflicted person. She then told her sisters who went to assist the sick not to lend themselves only for temporal care, but to comfort in every way, pointing out the hope of supernatural goods. I heard her many times comfort the poor with good words, speaking to them of God, of eternal goods and of resignation. «We must love Jesus, she told them, seek Jesus, and he will never let us lack anything». When poor people presented themselves, complaining because they lacked everything, she told them: «This is the sign that you do not love Jesus enough. Love him and he will not let you lack anything». I recall that at the Villa Pontellini at Fiesole, where I was on holiday with the Servant of God, many poor people presented themselves and some of these in poor health. The Servant of God gave them alms with her own hands, accompanying it with holy words of comfort and resignation. And I recall that two or three persons went away healed, as I myself saw them come to thank the mother because they had been healed. I recall further that the Servant of God said to them: «Thank God and St. Anne».

One day a poor woman presented herself at that villa, a prey to despair, because she was with child and held for certain that the unborn child would be born dead, or else expire soon after, as had always happened to her in all her previous births, and therefore she said to the Servant of God: «If it happens to me so this time too, I give myself up to despair». The Servant of God had tender compassion for her and then added: «You must do one thing: you must be at peace, for all will go well». And she handed her an image of St. Anne. After seven or eight days that woman gave birth to a boy and all went well. Before the Servant of God left Fiesole, that woman brought her little son to see, all joyful and content.

§ 257
She avoided even light faults for love of God.

Charity toward God: Of the charity of the Servant of God much already appears from what I have said so far, and certainly there is no question of speaking of grave faults of hers, but I am also persuaded that in her whole life she always tried to avoid even the lightest faults.

During all the time I was with her, I never noticed the slightest defect, apart from this fact which I shall relate. I had come only a few days before to this house, and already had the office of Sacristan. The Servant of God was looking for the cornucopias for the altar, preparing the Church with a certain solemnity, since it had been closed about a year for restoration. The Sacristan who had been before me had left; I did not know where these cornucopias were. The Superior, questioned, did not know how to say anything either, and so the Servant of God, who saw the Altar deprived of a beautiful ornament for the reopening of the Church, said to the Superior in a slightly resentful tone: «You should know where these things are». I did not see in her, however, an act of impatience, nor did I hear any word that denoted anger, and when she went away she was not even serious, but appeared at ease. The Superior went at once to her room to ask her pardon, but the Servant of God, who had not given great weight to what had happened, interrupted her saying: «But no, there was no need for you to come to ask pardon for this; I said so because I thought you knew the things of the house, and not to reproach you», and she did not even allow her to kneel. I have related this fact not because I noticed in her some defect, but solely because it is the most notable instance of resentment that I noticed in her, though, as I said, it does not seem to me that there was any resentment at all. This shows how great was her meekness.

§ 258
She recommended scrupulously avoiding small faults.

Proc. fol. 782: She recommended earnestly to her Sisters to avoid small faults, because, she said, the devil does not begin with great things, but begins perhaps with a pin, and not only to her Sisters did she make this recommendation, but especially in the Novitiate, where she went once or twice a week. When she heard of some grave offense against the Lord, she made a sign of horror, and expressed it with a tremor and made the sign of the Cross on her forehead. «And let us pray, — she said, — for these sinners: we must make up with prayers for the failings of others». The Servant of God was always in the presence of God and united with Jesus; and one may say that she never said a word without some aspiration or ejaculation to Jesus in between. The devotions dear to her she tried to spread also among others, and she inquired further how they practiced this or that devotion and instructed them on the way to pray.

§ 259
While she prayed she paid no heed to anyone.

Speaking of God she was moved and did not know how to hide her tears well. When she prepared and gave thanks for Communion she could be heard sighing. During prayer she paid no heed to anyone. I noticed splendor around her body, and sometimes around her whole person in the time of her prayer, and always in the acts for Communion. And this splendor was such that sometimes she seemed a sun. The splendor was not always equal. From the other Sisters, however, except Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, I did not hear this splendor spoken of. The aforesaid Sr. Anna Camilla also spoke to me of the stigmata which, she said, the Servant of God had; to me, however, it is not known. In a word I can say this: that she loved Jesus so much that she seemed always in ecstasy.

§ 260
Most lively charity toward neighbor.

Proc. fol. 187: Charity toward neighbor: The love of God impelled the Servant of God to a most lively love of neighbor, and the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne was founded for the spiritual and temporal good of neighbor. Many things I have already said that reveal her ardent charity for others. Besides teaching and recommending to her Sisters to instruct in catechism both children and adults, I shall also speak of her institution of the Luigini in this our Church, who came every Sunday, and to them the Gospel was explained in the morning and the catechism after dinner. Now, however, for some years, the Chaplain who took care of it having failed, at the Servant of God's wish, this congregation has ceased. The Servant of God busied herself with children when she was still a girl, and always busied herself with them also when she lived in the world. She strove from then on to have first Communion made, especially by those boys and girls who had passed the usual age for such an act. When she knew some needy boy who wanted to become a priest, she herself helped him as best she could, and recommended him to others for assistance. And this she did always in her whole life. She also always helped other young people who were of a poor family, to put them in a position to procure an employment or a trade. I recall in particular a young man who was helped by her, and so was able to obtain the degree of lawyer.

§ 261
She was concerned for the conversion and spiritual good of her neighbors.

She took great pains with orphan girls, to place them in some institute; she therefore also provided them with a small trousseau, and if there was no way to obtain free admission to the Institute, she herself provided a small monthly subsidy. The Sisters who had recourse to her uncertain, doubtful, agitated were completely reassured by the Servant of God and left her room content. The Princess of Fitalia turned to her often for counsel and followed it; one may even say that the said Princess did nothing of importance without first having heard the Servant of God. I saw several persons who no longer wanted to know of either God or the church, who came to the Servant of God and by her were led back to Jesus; she always had some in hand, and used to say: «We must make more account of these strayed persons than of those who walk by themselves on the right road, and we must take greater care of them; so the Lord wills». She prayed and had others pray not only in general for sinners, but also in particular for this one or that, and had Communions of her Sisters applied for them too. She then took interest also in their perseverance and inquired, sometimes sending Sisters to get news. She also inculcated to her Sisters, especially the Superiors, that they should busy themselves with poor sinners. When she had workmen in the house, she called them to her and asked them all the particulars of their family, not only on the spiritual side but also the temporal. She took particular interest in their children, whether they had made first Communion, seeing to it that they did. I recall that the brother-in-law of the Princess of Fitalia had abandoned God. The Princess did everything so that he would come to Rome to speak with the Servant of God. Though unwillingly, he let himself be induced, and the Servant of God drew him to the Lord. After continuing in the life of conversion, he died a holy death some years ago. Many others she led to the Lord by her work and her word. When she went to some hospital run by our Sisters, she inquired whether there was anyone obstinate who refused the Sacraments, and then she set to work for their conversion and always succeeded. Sometimes these strayed patients were at first irritated by her exhortations and threw after her whatever was presented to them, such as a cup of broth, etc., but she took no offense, attributed the fact to their illness and returned to them with all gentleness and sweetness, until those unfortunates, attracted by her good manners, yielded. Many of them then said to her: «You ought, mother, to stay always here with us». And she comforted them, assuring them that she would not abandon them. These things about the hospitals I heard narrated by the present Mother General, by Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi, by Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, and by other Sisters who came here, whose names I do not now recall. The Servant of God was all content and happy when she was at the bedside of these sick sinners, and so as not to leave them she did not even go to eat.

p. 154

§ 262
She wanted a special charity to the poor to be done in the houses every Saturday.

Proc. fol. 795: Every Saturday she wanted bread or soup to be distributed to the poor at noon in this house, as in the others where possible, and on certain feast days she had pasta, sausages, and other meat distributed, as also on the last day of carnival. And this custom is still kept in our Institute. She also distributed linen, and when the resources ran out, she then turned to her benefactors saying: «My resources for the poor are exhausted». And to make this collection she did not hold back from writing to distant persons and also in America, and so came to the aid of the poor, who found her always ready to help them. I know that at times she helped, with all due regard, persons fallen on hard times who were ashamed to ask for alms. The particular alms she did not want known, especially for families fallen on hard times.

Woe if she learned that anything had been lacking for her sick Sisters! She told the Superiors of the houses: «If necessary, for the sick Sisters, pawn even the chalice».

§ 263
Prudent in everything, she took counsel in important decisions.

Proc. fol. 803: Prudence: I can say with all assurance that the Servant of God fled every and any occasion of sin; I never saw her a single moment idle, but always intent on the work of writing, sewing, knitting, or crochet, etc., or on prayer or speaking of God. Her recreations I always saw rather brief, and I never noticed useless talk. During the recreations themselves, while she spoke, she worked with the crochet hook for the poor. Some rare times in summer, in the evening, for barely half an hour, she walked in the garden.

When she had to make some decision, she first made long and serious reflection, and for the affairs of the Institute she consulted her Council. She also first prayed to know God's will, and to this end had the Community's Communions prayed and applied. Being near her, I was able to know these things well in many circumstances. I heard from the Servant of God herself that when she was still in the world she often took counsel with the Archbishop of Genoa or with her own Confessor. I know that outsiders too, Gentlemen and Ladies, came to the Servant of God for counsel. As far as I know, the Religious held the counsel of the Servant of God in high esteem, and had recourse to her in their doubts and agitations. Since I now recall it, I shall say that Mons. Leopoldo Franchi, having gone one day to the Servant of God, who was at Prato, and having entered into conversation with her about the Episcopate with which he would be invested (it was then said that he would be Bishop of Pistoia and Prato), the Servant of God told him that he would be Bishop, but not of Pistoia. In fact Franchi was afterward Bishop of Livorno. The Secretary of the said Bishop fell gravely ill once while he was in our house at Florence. The Superior, Sr. Anna Amante, was distressed for fear he would die in our house, and wrote of it to the Servant of God, who answered: «Be at peace, for the Secretary will not die in our house, but will recover», and so it happened. The said Secretary and the Sisters said that it was the Servant of God who had healed him, and I also heard it said, but cannot however vouch for the truth, that that Secretary said he had seen Gattorno in spirit during that illness, who said to him: «Be at peace, son, do not lose heart, for St. Anne will make you recover». During this vision he said that he saw the Servant of God; the Sisters, however, thought he was raving. He having then recovered, repeated the account of the vision, and then the Sisters believed him. The Sister who nursed that Secretary in his illness is no longer in the Institute now; for this reason I declared that I would not dare to vouch for the vision.

§ 264
She advised with calm and reflection.

She gave counsel with calm and reflection, as befits a serious and prudent person. Sometimes the Sisters who asked her counsel and had not yet had an answer asked for it again from the Servant of God, who answered: «Be at peace, in due time I shall give you the answer».

As far as I know, I think I can assure that the Servant of God never committed any imprudence in the government of the Institute, but rather governed it as an excellent and most prudent Superior. She knew how to deal with all according to their character: the more sensitive and delicate with delicacy, and the less so in a more brisk manner. So too she always used regard in reproving them, and never reproved them in the presence of the others; rather she added, after reproving them in her room: «Do not let the other Sisters notice, so they know nothing». In her ardent zeal for the glory of God, she did not let herself be carried away by fanaticism, but proceeded calm and resolute. When she gave counsel she never assumed the attitude of an important person, did not exaggerate, but did everything with simplicity.

p. 156

§ 265
She gave generously what she could. She practiced gratitude.

As to justice, I believe I can say with all assurance that the Servant of God never refused to give to others what she owed. Before dying she came to pay 40 thousand lire for the house of San Pier d'Arena, and was very glad, because she had proposed to settle that debt before dying. She imposed on the workmen who worked in this house, and had the Superiors impose on their workmen, to keep the feast holy. She then worked so that outside workmen too would keep it holy. She never gave offices or posts in the Institute from partial affection, but only in view of their being suited to the office to which she elected them. The Servant of God was most grateful toward those who benefited the Institute. Of the Lady who left the Gargatano estate to our Institute she kept her portrait on her desk to remember her more often.
