In memory of that Priest, benefactor of our house at Prato, who also gave the money to furnish the guesthouse of this house, she had a large portrait made to be kept displayed in the house at Prato. She then recommended to all her Sisters that they pray for benefactors, as she left written in the rules, and for deceased benefactors she also had Masses celebrated.

§ 266
Fortitude in decisions taken after praying and taking counsel.

The Servant of God was strong of soul, and when, after mature reflection, she had decided something, she let herself be moved by no motive. Already from when she was in the world she faced all difficulties and overcame them to carry out her holy desires.

I heard narrated by Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza and by the present Mother General and also by the late Sr. Anna Margherita, my companion at Prato, that the Servant of God did not hesitate to step over the body of her mother, stretched out on the doorstep to oppose her leaving; and she left the house to follow the will of God.

§ 267
Particularly strong in bearing difficulties.

She was much afflicted afterward, as I have related, by her relatives, but she was not broken in spirit. I have already spoken of the difficulty she had at the beginning of the Institute, but she never gave in and overcame them. When at times she saw the Institute slandered, she called the slanderers and with kindness said to them: «How can you say this?». And so she induced them to retract the slanders. She herself told it, and added that some of these had become benefactors of the Institute.

As for suffering, far from being downcast she was all content and said: «Woe to whoever touches a part of my Cross». The Servant of God was of a very lively character, but when I knew her the liveliness had gone, and I heard her say: «I who was of such a lively and cheerful character, never thought I would become like this, a limp rag». When something sad happened to her, on first learning of it by some letter or otherwise, she at once withdrew to her room, and after staying there some time, came out saying: «Well, let us do the will of God, the Lord wills it so». This I know because sometimes she said it to me, and added: «Pray».

§ 268
Most temperate in everything and always.

The Servant of God was most temperate. Her ordinary food was: potatoes, salt cod, stockfish. Sometimes salt-cod meatballs, without however pine nuts or currants. The present Mother General, thinking to do something pleasing, had fish salami brought to the Servant of God; but she, after tasting it, gave it away to Fr. Agostino Donadio. Her ordinary food was boiled greens; sometimes the cook added eggs to the boiled greens, but the Servant of God sent them back. As for quantity, nothing special, neither much nor little, except in her special times of penance, that is, in Lent, in Advent and on vigils, which she always kept most strictly: she ate at noon the soup, one dish only, and refused anything else the cook sent her. In the evening then of these days she ate nothing or almost nothing; she took a little soup more to be seen by the Sisters, who otherwise complained to her that she did not eat, than truly in order to eat.

At all times, moreover, her food was of such bad taste that to me it truly was not tolerable. Sometimes she called me near her and gave me a share, but I hoped she would never call me to taste that food. Once (she herself told me, and also the present Mother General) a Sister passed before her in the refectory while she was eating some rice granatine, and thought to herself: «Oh look, how well the Mother eats!». The Servant of God knew her thought, and having called that Sister she offered her some of those granatine, and she refusing out of delicacy, the Servant of God insisted so much that she was forced to take them. And having tasted them, she declared afterward that she had never eaten anything more disgusting. And the Servant of God said to her: «You see, and you think I eat well? You made a judgment that was not right».

Rice granatine are certain rice patties mixed with eggs and grated bread.

p. 158

§ 269
She slept very little.

Proc. fol. 813v.: The Servant of God slept very little; I was able to understand, speaking many times with her herself, that at night she had not gone to bed, and I was also able to understand it, and better still, from the present Mother General. The latter, seeing in the morning the great work accomplished by the Servant of God during the night, said to her in wonder: «But all this, Mother, when did you do it?». And she answered simply: «When I could». When she then went to bed I am sure she did not sleep more than two or three and a half hours. Not only I, but other Sisters too heard and saw her walking about the house, going to the Sisters' dormitories, etc.

§ 270
She was a great lover of personal and communal poverty.

Poverty: When, in the houses of the Institute where she arrived, she found that they had prepared a bed for her with fine blankets, she took them off immediately. Once, having arrived at the house in Florence, the Superior, Sr. Anna Amante, in order to keep them and preserve them apart, wished to prepare for the Servant of God two fine blankets for the bed, an armchair and a washstand. The Servant of God, on seeing these things, seriously reproved the Superior, observing to her that that was not for one who had made the vow of poverty, but for strangers and a hotel, and therefore at once removed those blankets from the bed and put the washstand and the armchair out of the room. As long as the Servant of God felt well, her pillows were of vegetable horsehair; then, having fallen ill, they were made for her of wool. I have already spoken another time of the iron chain, made like a crown, which she had at Piacenza. The furniture of the room at Piacenza I have already told another time. That of her bedroom here in Rome, here it is: two little fir tables with a black oilcloth over them, four ordinary rush-bottomed chairs, a washstand, an inkwell with pen, a Crucifix which is now in the Chapel adjoining this hall, a holy water stoup as is still there, a portrait of Sr. Anna Salvatore, and four pictures hung on the walls: one representing St. Anne, another the Sorrowful Mother, another brought her by the Polish Priest, of whom I have spoken, returned from America, the fourth, a memento of Cardinal Belmonte, returned, I think, from Paris. She had a metal clock given her by her son Alessandro. She had no prie-dieu in her room but knelt on the floor. The wardrobe of which I spoke the other time was not a piece of furniture but is built into the wall, with wooden doors.

p. 159

§ 271
She had only one habit to wear.

Proc. fol. 820: The Servant of God had only one skirt when she was a religious. When she died I looked among her things for another change of clothes to change her, but found only the one she always wore. When that habit needed to be washed, she handed it to me or to Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega before going to bed to be washed; it therefore had to be washed at once and dried so as to have it found near the door when she looked for it. Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega kept the things of the Servant of God in custody, and always kept ready, without her knowing, a bodice, that is a corselet, so that she would have one ready at once when the one she wore should be torn and frayed. She had to keep it without the Servant of God's knowing, because if the latter had known it, she would have scolded her and would not have permitted it. When afterward the bodice she wore was all worn out, Sr. Anna Benedetta replaced it with a new one, but the Servant of God complained and looked for the old one, and Sr. Anna Benedetta had to present it to her and make her observe the old one, which was absolutely unwearable, so that she would resign herself to the replacement. For fear that they would replace the skirt, or the bodice, or the scapular with some new one, in the evening she often mended these things herself, and said to me: «I have to do it myself, otherwise they replace me with a new one».

§ 272
It pleased the Servant of God to see the sisters content in poverty.

Cheerfulness pleased the Servant of God, and she wanted the Sisters to be always cheerful and content, but she herself was always moderate in speaking. She liked to joke affably. Here is one example. On the occasion of the Priestly Jubilee of the Supreme Pontiff, Leo XIII, this our House being full of Cardinals and Bishops, many Sisters were every day very busy and tired. One morning, about ten, the Servant of God went to the kitchen (where, moreover, she often went to see whether the cooking was good and everything well ordered) and, of seven or eight roast chickens that the cook had already prepared for the guests, took four and, having called the Sisters who were most fatigued: «For you, she said, take them», and promptly carved the chickens, dividing them among them, added a flask of wine, then said further: «Take bread and go and eat in the garden without letting anyone see you». It was a fine recreation for those poor things. When afterward the cook returned, who had not been present at the distribution of her chickens, she was desperate on seeing them gone, and ran to the Servant of God to relate her sad case. The latter feigned surprise and sympathized with the poor cook: «Go and look for whoever took them, — she said to her; — for the rest do not worry, they will have been given to poor people». The cook searched, but in vain. They laughed about it among the Sisters at the recreation after dinner. Then the Servant of God, having called the cook to her, asked whether she had found who had stolen her chickens, and what she would do to the one she learned was the author of this theft. The cook answered that she had not yet been able to trace her, and that on finding her she would scold her. «Well, — the Servant of God resumed, — it was I, I myself who gave them to those poor Sisters who were tired from all these days of toil; you certainly would not have given them, but I gave them».

Once the Servant of God said to the Sisters at recreation time: «Go and put on your aprons, for I want to take your portrait». The Sisters ran happily to put on the black apron, and one had already planned to send the photograph to her mamma, another to this person, another to that.

One said I want two, another three. «Yes, as many as you wish», answered the Mother. They arranged themselves in order for the photograph. The Servant of God declared that she would make one for the Professed and one for the Novices, «but the Novices must not be present when I do it for the Professed». All the Professed, then, prepared themselves. One asked permission to hold a book in her hand, another something else. «Whatever you wish», said the Mother. When all were ready, the Servant of God raised the box she held in her hand, which looked like a camera, inviting all to fix their gaze on it. Then the spring snapped and a donkey appeared, to the great hilarity of all. The next day she repeated the joke on the Novices. Sometimes she played other jokes, such as hiding from the cook the things carefully prepared on some extraordinary occasion for the Sisters. She recommended poverty greatly to the Sisters. I recall that once a Sister had bows of silk cords; the Servant of God had them removed and corrected her. Some Sisters wished to wear a skirt of tibet (fine wool) instead of scotto (coarse cloth). The Servant of God, if in visiting the houses she found some matter of this kind, at once remedied it by correcting, and obliged them to change cloth, and for fear that they would put on the tibet garment, sometimes had it handed over to her. Once, showing me a skirt of tibet, the Servant of God said to me: «This one I took from a Sister», telling me the name. Likewise she did not permit the Sisters to have fine linen. And so that every danger of departing from poverty in clothing might be removed, in this generalate house she made a storeroom for cloth and linen to which all the houses had to apply for supplies. And to this storeroom the houses of America must also apply. She never failed in the least against the vow of poverty when she was a religious.

§ 274
Already as a child she was distinguished by obedience.

The Servant of God was always most obedient, she never failed in the least against this vow when she was a religious.

Her mamma loved her dearly, precisely because she was so obedient, as I heard from her brothers, who loved her so much when she was little, because she was good and obedient to whoever commanded her. And she was moreover attentive to all from childhood. If at home she saw that something was needed, she at once lent herself, without anyone asking her. It has now come to my mind, regarding poverty, that at table she did not permit anyone silver cutlery, and having found it sometimes on visiting the houses, she removed it. Likewise she did not permit fine tableware.

I have already spoken of her deference to the Pope, the Archbishop, the Confessor, and in general the Superiors.

Proc. fol. 827v.: To the prescriptions of the ordinary doctor the Servant of God submitted; however, when she saw no result from the medicines prescribed her, she abandoned them, and sometimes said to me: «You see, they are no use; when the Lord does not will it, it is time lost». Her persuasion, however, before taking the medicines, was that they would do her no good; and yet she conformed.

The Servant of God was also deferential to her Sisters, and at times yielded to their ideas though she was of a quite contrary opinion.

§ 275
She avoided, and recommended avoiding, excessive familiarities.

Chastity: With her brothers the Servant of God never took too much familiarity, nor with the son-in-law; and when she went to the parlor for any person who had to speak to her, she always went accompanied. I never noticed in her the slightest act of curiosity when traveling. She did not permit newspapers of any kind to enter the houses of the Institute. I heard from the Servant of God herself that she insinuated to the Teachers that they should be attentive to the girls' books; and she herself wanted to see the books of the Postulants when they entered. For fear of profanation and mockery, she did not want illustrated postcards representing Saints sent through the Post Offices, neither open nor in envelopes; and when some arrived for her or for other Sisters, she took note in order to inform of her wish the persons who had sent them.

In the Circulars she sent each year she always recommended that the Sisters not give familiarity to the girls, that the nursing Sisters be reserved with other male and female nurses and with the other male staff of the hospital, and in general that no Sister ever give her hand to a man. These same recommendations she renewed when she saw the Superiors. «And when you notice a Sister who is light, — she told them, — try to correct her, and if then she does not heed you, inform me». She almost never spoke to me of her Marriage, except that time when I asked her whether at the celebration of her wedding she had worn the dress with a train. And another time again she told me that the muteness of her little daughter was due to her having taken a husband: «It is a punishment that has come upon me because I took a husband». The Servant of God felt as a humiliation having been united in marriage, so that I once said to her: «Why, Mother, are you ashamed of having taken a husband? it is not a sin; the Church permits it». And she answered me: «What do you want? I feel a certain repugnance». For this reason she never spoke of it, not even with the other Sisters. When the Servant of God came to know that a Sister was a little light, she put her under a skilled Superior, and first had her make the spiritual exercises, and used to say: «Then they mature with the years and improve». She did not bring herself to send them away from the Institute, and I do not recall that she sent any, except those two already named sent to Gargatano, because, she used to say, if they are not for the Institute, St. Anne takes care of sending them home. I do not mean by this to say that she did not send away Novices when she did not see them suited to the Institute.

§ 276
Prudence in dealing with men.

Proc. fol. 835: From what I have already said other times, about the Servant of God not wishing to go to the Parlor alone, nor to remain alone with men, though brothers and relatives; from her recommendations to all the Sisters never to give their hand to a man; and from so many other prescriptions preserved in the Rules, it clearly appears how jealous was her love for chastity. Regarding this virtue I do not at the moment recall any other particular fact. I can add that sometimes the Sisters having thought it proper to withdraw when her brothers came to visit her, to leave them freedom to speak, the Servant of God always complained of it to the Sisters and reproved them for having left her alone.

When she was in bed, even through illness, as in the last, she never wanted men in her room, except naturally the doctor and the Priest. Her brother Federico entered and remained in her room when the Servant of God was already in agony. And at the visit made by her brother Checco, of whom I spoke above, she, to receive him, rose from bed and went into the study.

§ 277
She loved humility greatly and practiced it.

The Servant of God was most humble. She loved to repeat often that she was a beast, a she-donkey. And I once saying to her: «You will be a donkey of Jesus», «No, no, — she answered, — if I were a donkey of Jesus I would be something». She loved to be despised, asked it of the Lord, and found herself content in humiliations and contempt. She said sometimes, in my presence, turning to the Lord: «My Jesus, what do you leave me here on earth for? I do nothing but sin; I am good for nothing but to offend you». She wished to appear ignorant, and to hear her, she knew nothing. If sometimes she made a mistake in speaking, or something was done badly for her, she was quick to point it out before the other Sisters, saying: these are my virtues; I am good for nothing, I am truly a beast who understands nothing, and other similar expressions. She never pointed out any good thing of hers, never spoke of it herself, and did not want to hear it spoken of by others.

I recall a time when I said to her: «You, Mother, are Foundress of an Institute». And she, to correct me resolutely but gently, almost to slap me on the mouth, put the back of her hand over my mouth saying to me: «Be quiet, chatterbox, what do you want to chatter about?». I have already said other things that reveal her humility in other sessions, in not wishing to be called Foundress either aloud or in letter.

Once I wished to kiss her hand, but she, with dexterity, turned mine toward me, so that I kissed my own and not hers. And she, all pleased with this joke: «From now on, she said, you will not try again to kiss my hand», for she did not want it kissed by anyone, and I do not remember whether she let it be kissed only by the Novices.

§ 278
When and how she let herself be photographed.

Proc. fol. 843v.: Ten years before dying, according to what was affirmed to me by the present Mother Gen., Benedetta Carrega, the Servant of God had her photograph taken. One day she was upset, and the Cardinal Protector was in her Study, and she was upset precisely with him. To disguise her upset with him, the Servant of God said to the Sisters present (probably Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza and Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega): «I want a portrait made of myself, call me a photographer. It is so long that the Sisters have been telling me, do I not do well, Eminence? (turning to the Cardinal)». And he, all pleased: «Oh! at last she has let herself be persuaded!». A photographer was therefore sent for at once, and the Servant of God was portrayed at the little table in that attitude, as seen in her portrait, placed before the articles of the Postulator. After some days the photographer brought the first copy to be seen, and the Servant of God said to the Sisters who presented it to her: «Throw it into the fire», and the Sisters in fact threw it into the fire, but had another made, which was circulated after her death. And so they could answer truthfully the Servant of God (who, preoccupied with that photograph, asked her Sisters some days later whether they had really carried out the command to burn it) by saying yes.

When I saw the photograph of the Servant of God, after her death, I was surprised and, turning to Mother Carrega, said: «Oh! how melancholy our Mother is! It seems they took it in the last times. But when did they take it, for I never noticed anything?». And Mother Carrega told me what I have reported above.

I must add that the Servant of God had truly been begged, many times, by her daughters to let herself be photographed, and the poor Sisters who left for America remained sorrowful because they did not carry with them the photograph of their Mother. Two other photographs were taken of her without her noticing. In one she stands in the act of rising from the desk, and in the other she sits, writing. The first I saw for the first time in Florence at Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera's, who kept it displayed in the parlor, taking care, however, to remove it from view when the Servant of God happened to be there. That the Servant of God was photographed secretly on those two occasions was confirmed to me also by other Sisters, besides Mother Carrega. Naturally, for fear it would become known to the Servant of God, not even these two photographs were circulated.

§ 279
She attained an uncommon degree in the practice of the virtues.

Ad 28: As to the degree the Servant of God attained in the exercise of all the theological and cardinal virtues, and of the others of which I have spoken, I believe I can assert calmly that the Servant of God attained a degree far superior to that attained by the other Sisters commonly esteemed very virtuous. And by the manner and constancy with which the Servant of God practiced them, I believe likewise I can assure that she practiced them as a true Saint, worthy of the altar, that is, as, and even better than, so many Saints whose lives I have heard read, and therefore in a heroic degree.

§ 280
She practiced the virtues without exaggeration.

Ad 29: The Servant of God, I can assert with all assurance, did not exceed in the exercise of any virtue, not even in that of mortification, making herself unfit for the fulfillment of her duties by excessive penance, and having fulfilled her duties completely to the last of her life; nor did zeal ever make her go beyond bounds by indiscreetly demanding too much of her Sisters.

§ 281
Prophecies and supernatural gifts.

Ad 30: I have already spoken of her prophecy about King Umberto, a prophecy expressed in these terms to me: «I am sorry that they want to kill the King». And my pointing out to her that it would be very difficult, because he had so many guards, she added: «And yet they will kill him». And so it happened the following year. Sometimes she told me: «This year, or the next, an epidemic comes», and she specified the kind of epidemic, smallpox, cholera. And my asking how she came to know it, she said to me: «It is the Lord who lets me know it by means of certain signs in the air, such as for example: black spots for diseases, and blood for wars». And once she predicted precisely a war. She also determined for me the places where these events would occur, and I verified that they always occurred every time. She then turned to the Lord to know the meaning. The reason she came to know such misfortunes beforehand seems to have been that she should pray and have others pray.

Ad 31, Proc. fol. 855: What I knew of miraculous healings or other miracles of the Servant of God I have already said. But now the following fact comes to mind. Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera once had a cancer in the breast, and the doctor had declared that she must be operated on. The Servant of God made a sign of the cross over her breast and the Sister was healed immediately. And when the doctor returned to visit her, he found her cured. This fact occurred when I was already residing in Rome.

§ 282
Peritonitis, the proximate cause of her death.

Proc. fol. 860v.: The proximate and immediate cause of the death of the Servant of God was a peritonitis, developed four days before her death. But already earlier she was swollen, and I heard it said that the blood was turning into water.

She also had tumors in the abdomen and the heart too was not functioning well.

About two months before dying, the Servant of God began to see the signs foretelling her death. The first sign was the sight, three or four times, of blood in the clock she kept on the table. Every time she saw this sign it was about midnight, and every time she, who was already in bed because in poor health, showed me, who was assisting her, that sign, saying to me: «Look, look at that blood in the clock. It is the blood I shall give after my death». I too saw that blood, and answered the Servant of God: «Oh come! you are always thinking of this». And she to me: «And yet…», in a tone of assurance.

§ 283
Serenity during her last illness.

Proc. fol. 998: On the Friday that preceded her death, in the midday hours, the Servant of God said to me: «Where are the Sisters? Call them for me a moment». I ran to the Secretariat, but finding no one there I went along the corridor and, seeing some Sister climbing the stairs, said to them: «Come, come at once to the Mother, she wants you», and there arrived in the Mother's room seven or eight, among them the present Mother General, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, Sr. Michelina Negri, Sr. Anna Giuseppina Tornatore.

To the Sisters present the Mother then said: «I thank you for all you have done for me. Now everything is averted for me».

And this she said showing herself relieved and content, so that we interpreted those words in the sense that she would soon recover. And we expressed to the Servant of God our joy, saying to her: «So, Mother, now you are a little better? let us hope you will recover!». And she answered: «Yes, now I recover». She smiled and added nothing more. The Sisters, however, not having remained completely at ease, charged me to try to learn from the Servant of God the true meaning of her words. And I in fact did what I could to discover from the Mother what she meant precisely, and said to her: «The Sisters have left all content; one sees that you are already a little better: so you recover, is it not so?». She smiled at me, but not answering me anything, I added: «But how is it that you do not answer me?». Then she answered: «I would not know what to answer you: poor daughters, you are mistaken».

The Sisters of the Secretariat were waiting for me in the Mother's study, awaiting my informing them of the explanation given me by her; and having come out, I informed them. I remember that the present Mother General, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza and Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini were present. I remember that these last two said: «Ah yes, the Mother feels she is dying». Those words, that everything is averted, meant that for her the toil of life was over.

Toward the evening of that same Friday, the Servant of God showed a desire to have in her room the image of Mary Mater Gratiae, Mater misericordiae, which was in the Chapel adjoining this hall, and it was brought to her with its whole throne. Then she got out of bed and, standing, leaning, made a prayer to that image for about ten minutes. It must be noted that the Servant of God wore in bed a long nightshirt, which was like a robe. The Sisters present (about five or six, among them certainly Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini), noticing that that prayer was lasting a little too long, would have liked to tell her to lie down, but no one dared. I must observe that when the Servant of God was getting ready to get out of bed, almost all the Sisters present withdrew outside, leaving the door open, and looked in from time to time to see whether the Mother had gone back to bed. Having gone back to bed, the Servant of God said to us:

§ 284
Last confession and holy Viaticum.

«Prepare everything, for now I would like to receive Communion as Viaticum». We were stunned, and tried to dissuade her, telling her that she was not in an alarming state; but she replied: «Oh! must one then receive Viaticum only when one is altogether ill?». The Viaticum was therefore brought to her at nine that evening by Fr. Agostino Donadio.

A couple of days before she had confessed to Fr. Vincenzo, Capuchin. The Viaticum was the last communion she made, she being no longer able to receive Communion, no longer being able to swallow, and she felt like vomiting; they said: «Here an internal paralysis has come upon her»; and the Sisters said: «Fortunate that she received the Viaticum, for today it would no longer have been possible for her».

Doctor Montechiari, the attending physician, from ten or twelve days before her death had declared to the Sisters of the Secretariat that there was no longer any hope, although the Mother went to the Secretariat until the Wednesday, after dinner, preceding her death. Indeed on the Wednesday, I recall, she dined in the study; then she went no more, because she grew worse and efforts to vomit manifested in her.

From the night of that Wednesday on, every night it was no longer I alone who assisted her, but there was always some other Sister with me. This she noticed, and said: «What novelty is this of such a coming and going of Sisters? One sees I am worse».

We tried to make her believe there was nothing alarming and that other Sisters coming to assist her should not surprise her. But she replied: «But I already know it, that I am dying. What does this mystery mean?».

Doctor Montechiari, although persuaded of the Servant of God's approaching death, had however never expressed his thought to her, not even on Friday evening, after having visited her, when he said to the Sisters of the Secretariat: «It is much if the Mother lasts another twenty-four hours».

So swollen was our mother that the doctor had said to our Sisters: «I fear the Mother will burst on you while still alive». It was on the Wednesday that preceded her death, when she began to grow much worse, that I removed from the Servant of God the chain that encircled her whole waist and which was embedded in her flesh because of the swelling, and of this I have already spoken. From the morning of Saturday on, the Servant of God could no longer make herself understood, though she tried to pronounce words, because, I believe, of the swelling of the tongue. I recall that about seven or eight in the morning, her brother Checco having come to her room, she wanted to tell him something, but it could not be understood.

The image of Mary Mater Gratiae that had been brought to her on Friday was first placed on the little table beside her bed; then she had it placed on the little foot table to be able to see it more comfortably, and that Friday night and throughout Saturday I observed her many times fold her hands and, looking at Our Lady, pray to her. On Saturday evening then, by means of signs, she made it understood that she wanted Our Lady again on the nearer table, and, the image brought to her by Fr. Agostino who was present, she got out of bed again, as the day before, and prayed a brief moment to Our Lady, and then lay down again, saying: «Now I shall not get up again», and these words were the only ones that could be understood distinctly during the whole day of Saturday, and then she spoke no more. Before the image of Our Lady she wanted two candles always kept lit, and when they tried to put them out, she made a sign that they should relight them; and, asked whether their light bothered her, she made it understood that it did not.

When she was getting ready to rise to make the last prayer to Our Lady, some Sisters were of the opinion to prevent her, but another pointed out that it was better to leave her this last consolation.

In getting out of bed she let no one help her, as also the evening before. To lie down again, however, we helped her a little. Yet I must note that it helped a great deal that her bed was very low.

§ 285
Anointing of the Sick.

On Saturday evening, Fr. Vincenzo, Capuchin, having asked her whether she desired Extreme Unction, she made a sign of yes; it seems to me it was about nine o'clock when it was administered to her. And the Servant of God received it with great devotion, accompanying the ceremony. I must note that when she was asked whether she wanted Extreme Unction, she was asked whether she received it willingly; she, to show her pleasure, made a sign not only with her head but also with her hands.

Many Sisters were present at her Extreme Unction, among whom I recall Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera and Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini. The Servant of God being asked whether she desired the Blessing of the Holy Father and having given an affirmative answer, it was requested and obtained immediately from the Vatican. She then entered into agony and made no more sign (except sometimes opening her eyes) until death.

§ 286
Serene agony and death of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 1008v.: From Saturday evening, when the Servant of God entered into agony, until death, Fr. Vincenzo, Capuchin, never moved from our house, going to sleep only some hours in the night, and Fr. Agostino Donadio, Paolotto, went in and out of the Servant of God's room, never leaving. On Saturday evening there came to see her her brother Federico, her daughter with her husband and Nonni, who stayed until about midnight, except Nonni who remained during the time when her father Count Barbiellini took his wife back home.

The Servant of God expired at nine in the morning, and her soul rose and moved upward in the midst of this cortege of angels and Saints.

I saw the soul of the Servant of God white as a dove. It was very beautiful, but did not have that splendor that the other Saints had. As soon as it left the body it said to me: «Farewell, Serafina; in eight days you will be with me, if it is God's will».

I must note that many times I had said to the Mother: «When you have died, pray the Lord to make me die too. What shall I do here without you?». I was all content at her words, but, all moved, I began to weep, and said to the other Sisters: «You know, the Mother is dead». I must observe that the Mother had made no movement, so they did not believe she was dead, and answered me: «But what? She is not dead yet». And my replying again: «Yes indeed, she is dead», Sr. Anna Camilla said: «Let us feel a little how the extremities are», and, feeling that the extremities were quite warm, they were confirmed in the idea that she was not dead.

Yet Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera said: «But here her hands are cold as ice, and they are heavy. How is this mystery?». I replied that the Mother was dead. A little candle was taken and brought near her lips; the flame was seen not to move. They were then persuaded that the Mother was dead.

§ 287
Strange behavior of the relatives beside the deceased.

As soon as the Servant of God expired, Nonni entered the room and went straight to rummage in the pockets of the Servant of God's habit, and took with her the little book, as I have already related. Then, turning to the corpse of the Servant of God, with her hand stretched out over the body, at the foot of the bed, she said these words: «As grandmother I respect you, as Mother General I file a complaint against you. In my grandmother I never had trust». And she went out.

Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, present at these words, felt ill. Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera said: «She deserves two slaps». And Count Barbiellini, to excuse his daughter, said: «Do not be astonished nor scandalized, they are words said in a moment of bitterness».

Present also was the Notary Monti, called there immediately, who, at Nonni's words, turned pale. The Apostolic Visitor, now Cardinal Serafini, had sent his Secretary Don Ambrogio, Benedictine. Count Barbiellini, the Servant of God having expired, declared that everything was his; but the Notary Monti having pointed out to him that a will existed, which also had to be respected, he turned pale and, turning to Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, said to her: «I shall make her go through so much, as long as I live». These words were said outside the room of the Servant of God. However, having re-entered, it was in the presence of two witnesses and, the Notary drawing up the Minutes, an inventory was made of what was found in the room of the Servant of God, and the will of the Servant of God was read forthwith. Among other things was found also the receipt for the fifteen thousand lire that the Servant of God had given her granddaughter Nonni on the occasion of her marriage, and which she with great effrontery still claimed, as if they had not been given to her.

The dust that covered the papers and the two little boxes of the Servant of God was there to testify, as the Notary Monti pointed out to Count Barbiellini, who dared to say that the Sisters had stolen everything, that on the contrary the Sisters had touched nothing.

§ 288
Signs of penances on the corpse.

I myself dressed the Servant of God, helped by three other Sisters: Sr. Anna Consolata, present Provincial of Upper Italy; Sr. Anna Rosella, surname, I think, Bolognini, now deceased; and the then Mistress of Novices, now likewise deceased, whose name I do not recall. On that occasion we found on the upper part of her chest several rows of scars, which had already healed some time before; likewise on the two forearms and the two arms there was a row of scars of many little dots. On the left side of the rib cage I found something like a cut, which I saw to be rather deep, but did not observe well. It was of a violet color: I washed it like all the rest of the body. Since in this operation I did the principal part, I tried to hide it from the other Sisters, who therefore did not see it.

§ 289
Difficulty in photographing the Servant of God because of the blood.

Proc. fol. 1018v.: When afterward, the next day, about two in the afternoon, the body was moved to be put in the coffin, then she emitted more, so that she stained her whole habit. Because of this blood the photographer had great difficulty in taking her image, since, however much he tried to clean it, it appeared always anew, and a brief moment had to be seized in which it seemed to give respite so that she could be portrayed; but even in that portrait it is understood by us, who know the thing, that the blood had not ceased, and on one side of the mouth the blood is seen.

I said that the emission of blood from the mouth lasted about twenty-four hours; but really I could not determine the duration, because, placed in the coffin, she was covered with the same sheet and wool blanket with which they had lifted her from the bed and put her in the coffin, and covered still with a black veil, and placed beside her a metal tube, which I do not know what it contained, a prayer book and that of the Rule and a written note brought by Count Barbiellini, who asked that it be placed, I think, in the tube; the coffin was closed, and we did not see her again.

To place her in the coffin was no small struggle, because the body had swollen enormously, so that it barely fit. The first coffin was naturally of wood, the second of lead, the third, outer, of walnut. The third coffin was used only an hour before her transport to the cemetery, but when they went to place it in this third one of walnut, the lead one had swollen so much that it did not fit into the walnut one. Then the tinsmith made a hole, I do not remember well on which side, and from it there came out evidently a dense gas, which had the appearance of smoke, making noise, like the whistle of a train, which lasted about a quarter of an hour, and left for about a month a brick beside the coffin stained a dark color, although I tried several times to clean it, and in the end I used pumice, with which finally I managed to see it clean. This gas had no bad smell. As soon as placed in the two coffins, the body was carried to the Chapel adjoining this hall, where it remained until seven or eight o'clock the next day, when it was carried into our public Church, where it remained until about two in the afternoon.

§ 290
Veneration of the people toward the body of the Servant of God.

Ad 34: When after the washing the Servant of God was re-clothed, free passage was left to the people who came to see her; and until she was carried to the Cemetery people always flocked. And when they could touch her corpse, they brought medals, crucifixes, rosaries, handkerchiefs close to her, and when she was placed and closed in the coffin, they brought these objects close to the coffin. The Sisters then cut her hair, so that I cried out at them, because, moving her a little, more blood always came from her mouth, but they, poor things, did it to keep a memento of their Mother.

To see the Servant of God, I recall, all sorts of people came: priests, religious, laypeople, Daughters of Mary of our Congregation, their mothers, gentlemen and ladies; in short, all who knew her came to see her before she was placed in the coffin, and then at the funerals. There was a continual coming and going of people, until she was placed in the public Church. And I can assure you that perhaps a thousand and more people came to visit her. And when the first funerals were held, there was a great concourse of people of every class and condition.

Proc. fol. 1025v.: At the first funerals I must note that there were no special invitations, as were made for the funerals of the thirtieth day. But nonetheless the Church was packed full, and so it was also at the funerals of the thirtieth day, at which the Mass was pontifical, celebrated by the Apostolic Visitor, and the funeral oration was read by Mgr. Sardi. The Visitor did not permit the printing of the funeral oration.

§ 291
Burial at the Campo Verano.

Ad 35: In the afternoon hours she was transported to the Campo Verano, accompanied by many Capuchins, by many Sisters of our Institute, by the Daughters of Mary, by many gentlemen and ladies and by many other people. And this cortege did not leave her until the Campo Santo. She was then placed in the common tomb of our Institute, where she remained for a year, and then was placed in a chapel built expressly for our Institute, in Via delle Cappelle, on the old Pincetto, and with her were placed all the other Sisters who lay in the old tomb. The Servant of God, however, was placed at the entrance door.

§ 292
Graces attributed to the Servant of God.

Ad 36: I forgot to say in the preceding Interrogatory that I heard it said by the Daughters of Mary, and by some of my Sisters in religion, whose names I could not now specify, and by other people of the populace, that shortly before the Servant of God was transported to the cemetery, some sick persons entered the Church to pray before her body and commend themselves to her, and that, feeling themselves cured, they joined the cortege and accompanied her as far as the Campo Santo. Certainly I was told of at least two cured; I could not assure that there were more persons.

Another particular I had forgotten: men and women approached the coffin while it was being placed on the funeral carriage, and kissed it. At that moment the son-in-law and his daughter Nonni, who stood six or seven meters away, said in a quite intelligible voice, so that many persons, among them I, heard it: «Oh! what are you going to kiss that coffin for? she is no Saint! She lies seven palms below hell».

Going many times to the Campo Santo (I go there every fifteen days at least, also to clean the Chapel, and before I went every week), I noticed that, attached to the upper gate of the Chapel, there were almost every time fresh flowers placed there I know not by whom, and often also little lamps. And these, certainly, neither flowers nor lamps, were placed there by our Sisters, because when they go there they always ask me for the key of the Chapel, and I never noticed there acts of worship permitted only to Saints, nor did I notice other acts of worship when, dead, she was laid out, carried to the Church and in the transport to the Campo Santo.

Sometimes I found people praying before the upper gate of the Chapel.

I must note that in the upper part of the Chapel there is only the Servant of God, while the other Sisters rest in the lower Chapel, the tomb of our Institute being composed of two chapels, one above the other, both with distinct accesses and gates.

Sometimes, having asked those persons whom I had found praying before the upper gate whether they had known our Mother, I heard this answer: «We did not know her; we have heard, however, that here there is a Saint, and we have come to pray to her to obtain a grace».

Once a priest, another time a Sister of our Institute, now deceased, and two or three other times other persons, sent me wreaths of flowers in metal with this inscription: «For grace received», to hang before the sepulcher of the Servant of God, and I hung them; four or five other silver hearts were brought to me by other persons, for graces received, to hang likewise before the sepulcher of the Servant of God. But I answered these persons: «Now they cannot be put before the Mother, because she is not canonized», and suggested that they have me put them before Our Lady or St. Anne, which was granted me.

A certain Fr. Agostino of the Friars Minor Franciscan, residing in the Convent of St. Anthony, near here, told me and the other Sisters one day that, passing one day before the sepulcher of the Servant of God, he could not help stopping to commend himself to her prayers.

§ 293
Reputation for holiness before and after death.

Ad 38: Therefore it is within my knowledge that not only the Sisters who knew and approached the Servant of God esteemed her a Saint, but also other people of the populace; I can say indeed that many people and also distinguished and respectable persons esteem her a Saint and say that one day she will be on the Altars. I have heard it said many times, by all sorts of persons, priests included: «Blessed are you, who knew and approached the Mother Foundress».

The Princess of Fitalia, then, always declared to me that she never turned to Mother Gattorno without being heard.

I too pray to her always every day, and when there is something that interests me particularly for the Institute, I pray to her more than usual, and I can declare that she has always obtained for me from God what I desired.

§ 294
The family's claims to annul the will.

Proc. fol. 1034: The relatives of the Servant of God then brought other suits, claiming the annulment of her will, and that the donation of the Gargatano estate had not been made to the Servant of God but to her daughter Carlotta, and that our Houses of Rome in Via Merulana, of Florence, of Piacenza and of Naples belonged to the daughter Carlotta, and the house of Sampierdarena fell to Nonni.

I know that they first turned to the Ecclesiastical Tribunal and then to the Civil.

The vicissitudes of these suits dragged on until 1912, with the complete victory of our Institute; or, better said, the Institute, which was pleased to see everything ended, resigned itself to undertaking, I think, to pay five thousand lire a year to Carlotta, daughter of the Servant of God, for life.

Proc. fol. 1053v.: From the Sisters I have always heard her spoken of with great veneration, with the esteem of a Saint, of a woman of spirit, of a woman of great intelligence, and as a person who one day would be sanctified by the Church; and that the Institute would never in the future have such a woman. And all the Sisters I have heard speak believe that our Mother will one day be sanctified. I heard further from all the Sisters with whom I spoke on the matter that the Servant of God, during her life, worked graces, and it seems also after death.

The reputation for holiness the Servant of God enjoyed in our Institute during her life, and after her death this reputation increased.

From some Sister, however, I heard it said: «Our Mother was truly a Saint; a pity, however, that there were around her those blessed relatives, who perhaps one day will be a stumbling block to her sanctification. For the rest, on her own account she would have been worthy of being placed on the altars immediately after her death». They excused the Servant of God, however, because she was a mother, and the mother of an unfortunate daughter, whom she therefore could not abandon.

And the Church, they said, would take these considerations well into account, and in the end even this stumbling block would be overcome.

This reputation did not arise from the Sisters or others, but from having seen and noted the virtues she practiced.

As for persons outside our Institute, I do not recall whether it was spoken of, but outside too she enjoyed a reputation for holiness among all who knew her. I recall the Princess of Fitalia, her husband, her sister. I personally could not cite other persons outside our Institute, because I have contact with no one, but I have heard it said by the Sisters that universally the Servant of God was and is esteemed as a Saint, also outside the Institute.

With however many persons outside the Institute I have spoken, all told me that our Mother was a holy woman; I do not know then whether they meant a saint for the altar.

It is not known to me that anyone has done any work to conceal errors or defects of the Servant of God (e.g., by suppressing some writing of hers) or to exaggerate her virtues.

Ad 40: The Mother General still told me this fact: a Sister of our Institute (I recall neither the name nor the house)

p. 177

§ 296
Cure of a cancer attributed to the Servant of God.

had a cancer in the breast and the surgical operation was decided, and the instruments had been prepared for the next day. In the night that Sister commended herself to the Servant of God and placed on the diseased part a portrait of hers. Having fallen asleep, she saw in a dream the Servant of God, who said to her: «My daughter, you have nothing more». And she made over her the sign of the cross on the diseased part. Awakening, she felt no more pain at all, and there was no need of an operation. I do not remember other details.

Et expleto examine super Interrogatoriis, interrogata fuit Testis super Articulis (Proc. fol. 1084v.), super quibus sequentia deposuit.

From the first article to the twentieth I refer to what I have already stated, not recalling anything else.

As to the twentieth, where it is said that the Servant of God takes the most active part in order to develop the beneficent institution of the Daughters of Mary, of which she was the Directress, I must add that the Servant of God herself told me that the Archbishop of Genoa had charged her with drawing up the rules for the said Pious Union, and that, as she set about the work in obedience, Our Lord Himself dictated it to her.

She then became very worried because she did not want to tell anyone that Our Lord had dictated it to her; yet, reflecting well, she persuaded herself that she had to tell her Confessor, and he in turn imposed on her that she tell the Archbishop too when bringing him the written rule.

When she was telling me this fact, I ventured to say to her: «Who knows now how many letters Our Lord comes to dictate to you!». But she answered me: «Then I was better; but now that I am bad, He no longer comes».

Et proseguendo Ad Art. 163 (Proc. fol. 1094), testis respondit: I must confirm that several times she tried to withdraw from the burden of Superior General, and I recall that once Cardinal Protector Alimonda, once Cardinal Verga, once Cardinal Berardi and another time Pius IX himself imposed on her that she continue.

§ 297
Particulars of the witness.

My name is Domenico, son of the late Luigi and of Costanza di Pietro. I was born in Rome on 6 August 1852. I entered the Religion of the Benedictines of Subiaco in 1871, made simple vows in 1874 and solemn vows in 1877.

In 1877 I was ordained priest by Cardinal Monaco at Subiaco; then I was Master of Novices at the Abbey of San Giuliano in Genoa, then Prior at Santa Scolastica in Subiaco, then Procurator General in Rome, at Sant'Ambrogio, and in 1896 Abbot General.

I was then elected Archbishop of Spoleto in 1900, then Apostolic Delegate in Mexico in 1904, and I remained there for a year; I then returned to Spoleto, which I left in 1911, when I was appointed Assessor of the Holy Office and received the archiepiscopal title of Seleucia in Syria. I was created Cardinal, with the title of Santa Cecilia, this year, in the Consistory of 28 May.

§ 298
Scope of knowledge and esteem for the Servant of God.

Ad 7: I met the Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, Rosa Gattorno, only when I was appointed Apostolic Visitor of her Institute, an appointment which I think took place in 1897.

Before the Apostolic Visitation I do not recall that anyone ever spoke to me of Mother Gattorno, except a penitent of mine, a sister-in-law of the Servant of God herself, by the name of Amalia Custo, deceased many years ago, who, as I was about to take up residence in Rome, said to me incidentally and without my questioning her: «You are now going to Rome; there is a certain Rosa Gattorno there, who passes herself off as

p. 179

a Saint and deceives everyone: see whether you can undeceive those who have been misled».

I paid no heed to her words, above all because she was a ready talker. I learned afterward that there was friction in the family over matters of money.

In 1897, when His Eminence Isidoro Verga, Protector of the Sisters of St. Anne and Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, called me to entrust me with the task of the Apostolic Visitation of the Institute of the said Daughters of St. Anne, he said to me: «See if you can remedy those disturbances that are in that Institute: I am losing my head over it».

What those disturbances were he did not tell me.

That same Cardinal told me that several appeals had reached him, without specifying their nature. As I saw afterward, the appeals came from within the Institute, nor do I know that the relatives made any appeal either before or during my apostolic visitation. There was no good blood between the Sisters and the relatives, because the Sisters (I speak of the principal ones, such as the Superiors and Provincials) did not look with pleasure on the continual coming and going of the relatives, who had their dwelling both here in Rome and in Piacenza, adjoining that of the Sisters.

Ad 8: I have esteem for the Servant of God, as a woman of piety, of an uncommon mind and of much energy. I must say, however, that when the present Mother General of the Daughters of St. Anne turned to me for advice on introducing the Cause of Gattorno, I advised against it, though I presented that advice against it in a delicate manner.

§ 299
First meeting of the witness, Apostolic Visitor, with the Servant of God.

Ad 25: Appointed Apostolic Visitor, knowing that the Servant of God was at Piacenza, I went there, and at Parma I had my brother, then Abbot of San Giovanni, board the train with me and accompany me. Arrived at the house of the Daughters of St. Anne, and announced to the Servant of God as two Benedictine Abbots, she presented herself to us accompanied by three Sisters, saying: «These are my assistants: the Duchess Sorrentino, the Marchioness Carrega, and another whose name I do not recall».

Both to me and to my brother that curious way of presenting Sisters with their worldly titles made an impression. After the first compliments I stated the purpose of my visit and presented to her my appointment as Apostolic Visitor of her Institute. When she had read it, she came out with these words: «I already know that I am good for nothing, that I ruin everything, and therefore I resign from this moment», and she began to weep. I then tried to comfort her, assuring her that I had not come to destroy the work of God; that if I found everything well we would thank God together; that if there were something to correct we would correct it together and I would be of help to her; that I would then report to the Holy See and we would await its measures; and that there was to be no talk of resignations.

§ 300
The witness's impressions of the visit to Gargatano.

It was then agreed that the next day I would begin the hearing of the Sisters, and in fact the next day I began the hearing. The hearing lasted several days and was not easy for me, and I got to the bottom of nothing in that hearing. Only a vague, broken little word was said to me by the Provincial of Upper Italy, whose name I think was Sr. Anna Fortunata and who I believe is now deceased, being already old then. In those days a visit to Gargatano, proposed to me by the Servant of God, a visit which I made accompanied by the aforesaid Mother Provincial, made a bad impression on me; for there I found about 25 sick Sisters, who had lost their health in works for the Institute, assisted by other Sisters, who were sent there as a penance and therefore deficient in religious spirit. How could the poor sick women be assisted by those? It is true that there was a good Superior, but the religious assistance of the priest was very deficient, the nearest parish priest, who I think was about half an hour's walk away, having besides his own parish to attend also to the house of those poor sick women. I could not say anything else about that house, having been there only two hours. The impression I carried away was that those sick women were sheltered there, with the assistance of that personnel I have mentioned, in that countryside that had nothing else good but the air, perhaps so as not to leave unused that part of the house of Gargatano that had been given to her.

§ 301
The Sisters' distrust toward the Visitor.

At Piacenza I found the most complete distrust. But after a year or a year and a half a Sister from there wrote to me that at the beginning they had feared my visit, but that they had then become persuaded that I cared for nothing but the good of the Institute, and that therefore I should come back there,

p. 181

because they had several things to tell me that in the first Visitation they had kept silent.

It seems to me then that she added in that letter that they had been put on their guard, and that therefore they had kept silent. I do not recall who wrote it, nor can I say the moral worth of that Sister. Not having had the opportunity to return to Piacenza, I thought also that I could do without it, because it was not the individual small things to be modified, but the general course of the Institute.

The Visitation naturally being an odious thing, I tried to win hearts so as to gain confidence; thus I succeeded in finding some Sisters who opened themselves entirely to me and gave me light in my work.

§ 302
The witness was always treated courteously as Visitor.

I was always treated courteously, except in the house of Marcianise, where the Superior was an old companion of the Foundress. I must note, however, that she said nothing either against me or against the Holy See, but only vented herself against those who, according to her, persecuted the Servant of God. This was the only outburst she made, and nothing else.

Where I had to stay in their houses for lodging, I must say that I was treated with decorum. And on the whole I must say that, sooner or later, I won the trust and confidence especially of the Mother Provincials of Upper Italy, of Naples and of Palermo, the last in particular giving me light. I always found the present Mother General most correct, and if until the death of Gattorno she did not open herself entirely to me, it was out of deference to Mother Gattorno herself.

Distrustful toward me until her death I saw Mother Gattorno; yet I never received from her the slightest discourtesy.

§ 303
The Servant of God never opposed the good progress of the Visitation.

When I had some Sister called from other houses to speak to her, it was never refused me, not even under some pretext; nor can I know that they wished to remove those who were suspected of being contrary to Mother Gattorno. I did not always notify Mother Gattorno beforehand when I went to this or that house; e.g.: I would say to Mother Gattorno: «Now I am going to Naples», and when I was there I governed myself according to my own judgment, and according to what the Mother Provincial told me. So I did for Sicily and for Palermo and for Upper Italy.

Proc. fol. 881: With Mother Gattorno I was never in communication on internal matters of her spirit, and on this side therefore I do not know her, but only on matters pertaining to her government.

As to the idea the Sisters had of their Mother Foundress, I was able to speak of it with them a few times only incidentally and indirectly, and I asked them nothing about it in my visitation. From what, however, as I said, incidentally and indirectly, I came to learn, I discerned a great diversity of esteem among those sensible Sisters who stood out in the Institute for government.

Some esteemed the Mother as a woman of singular virtue, and attributed miracles to her as well, and among these were the Sisters who stood closest to Mother Gattorno. Others, on the contrary, esteemed her a good woman, but attributed nothing extraordinary to her.

I do not recall that among those Sisters who approached the Servant of God there was any who had a poor opinion of her.

The debatable points that I can know about Mother Gattorno, and which I came to know by reason of my mission as Apostolic Visitor, concern external matters, that is, the financial administration of the Institute and her manner of governing. And first of all as to the administration.

§ 304
Answers of the Servant of God to the Visitor's difficulties about the administration.

The administration of the Institute being wholly concentrated in the Generalate House, I asked it for the accounts, and saw that every year closed with a deficit, which, however, I did not see carried forward into the following year. Adding up all these deficits, a total resulted that I could not now specify, but which I think was about ninety thousand lire. I repeat, however, that I do not remember the figure well. I thought that if they proceeded at this pace, accumulating the deficits every year, the Institute would soon find itself in a bad way. Mother Gattorno being questioned by me about it, she told me that every deficit was balanced, and when I replied that there must then be another book showing the truth of the financial position, she answered me that no other book existed; that that was the only and true one, that that deficit was covered. And when I asked in what way it had been covered, she answered me that this was a secret that she would never reveal to anyone. And this was always her answer, though I insisted, set before her her duty to obey, since I came to her in the name of the Holy See, and though I also did not fail to make some threat to her.

p. 183

Some of the Sisters, as I learned afterward from the Provincial of Sicily and from Mgr. Sardi, in the funeral eulogy he made of Mother Gattorno, said that in covering the deficits that formed every year in the Institute's accounts there was something of the miraculous.

And the Provincial of Palermo added: «But I believe, on the contrary, that it is a very human thing».

Mgr. Sardi alluded in his funeral eulogy to this divine intervention in the financial straits of the Institute. Asked by me from whom he had learned it, he answered: «From the Sisters».

The words said to me by the Provincial of Sicily led me to discover that in the houses of the Institute the Superiors practiced too many economies, asked of their Sisters more than their strength could give, and this in order to be able to send, on various occasions, extraordinary sums to the Mother General as a gift (besides the accounting, half-yearly, I think, in which each House sent to the Generalate House the surplus of its cash), in the persuasion of thereby being more pleasing to the Mother General.

The Provincial of Palermo also told me that invitations went out from the Generalate House with the aim of obtaining these extraordinary remittances of money.

§ 305
Lack of necessities in some communities.

In the various houses I visited I found in some of them Sisters who suffered from lack of necessities. In a quite particular way I must make observations in this regard about the house of the Novitiate of Naples, where those Sisters truly suffered a great deal, especially from too much work; and I was assured that the Novices, as many as three times in one same day, were sent to accompany the dead.

I expressed for this many times my wish, without giving a formal order, that the Superior of that house be changed, because there was a consequent dissension between the Provincial and the local Superior, and for other reasons that I could not now specify, but I could not obtain it until Gattorno was dead, she maintaining that that Sister did so much good.

I must note that between the local Superior of the novitiate of Naples and the Provincial there was a little jealousy over reasons of preference with the Mother General.

The Houses of Sicily I found in much better order than those of Naples, and that Provincial took care in every way that those Sisters should not suffer lack of necessities, and I know that Mother Gattorno was very content with her houses in Sicily.

I noting (I do not recall well with which of the Sisters) that the Houses of Italy could send little money to the Generalate House, it was answered me, I do not recall by whom, that it was especially the Houses of America that sent money. I cannot say that I learned this also from some Superior of the Houses of America. I have ascertained, however, that thousands came from America, both as ordinary revenue and as extraordinary offerings.

§ 306
The Visitor's suspicion that the Servant of God was not well informed.

In short, the system was general. To the question put to me, whether Mother Gattorno herself knew that some Superiors, to make themselves more pleasing to her, made their communities go short, in order to send her more money, I would not know how to answer. I have a vague suspicion that Mother Gattorno was not informed in full detail of everything that happened around her.

This money that came to Mother Gattorno was certainly employed for the purpose of maintaining the Institute. Of this I am sure: it was not a matter of business, nor of enriching the relatives.

§ 307
Concern for numbers at the expense of formation.

As to the religious and spiritual part, it seems to me that in that Institute and in Mother Gattorno there was a concern to make numbers. Seeing in the Institute in general much lack of formation, of religious culture, I made this speech one day to Mother Gattorno: «Since you have already gathered a good number of Sisters, it would be good, in my opinion, to make a pause in accepting new ones, to take greater care of the spiritual assistance of these and of their formation and religious culture; and thus to consolidate the Institute a little better».

These speeches I made in the last months of her life. Mother Gattorno, uneasy, answered me: «But how? I hope that the Lord will grant me to see my Institute grow like the stars of heaven and the sands of the sea».

From the agitated manner in which the Servant of God answered my words, I supposed, and I suppose even now, that the Servant of God did not understand well the meaning of my words, and that she believed I wanted to hinder the development of her Institute.

Asked whether Mother Gattorno did not realize the com-

p. 185

§ 308
Perhaps the Servant of God was unaware of the Sisters' complaints.

plaints of her Sisters on the occasion of her visits to the Houses, I must observe that the Apostolic Visitation took place in the last years of Gattorno's life. Then, that, going on her visits accompanied, it may very well be that her Sisters did not enjoy all that freedom that was necessary to open themselves.

Proc. fol. 889v.: I could not say anything about the hearings that Mother Gattorno held in her visits, nor whether she held them alone or in the presence of some other Sister.

§ 309
Houses accepted without the necessary spiritual care.

I noted further that Mother Gattorno accepted Houses in Southern Italy, although there could not be that spiritual assistance on the part of the Clergy which was necessary for Sisters.

Then I observed still another fact, to my regret. Having gone, for my Apostolic Visitation, to Cornié, province of Alessandria, I think it was precisely at the Hospital of Cornié that I noted the following (if it was not precisely at Cornié, certainly it was in a municipality of the Province of Alessandria). The administration of the Hospital, in asking for the Daughters of St. Anne for that hospital, had set as a condition that the Sisters should not be changed without the authorization of the Hospital's Administrators themselves. At first Mother Gattorno refused, and then yielded. And this the Chaplain of the hospital himself told me, as if it were a triumph of his obtained for the good of the hospital, as if he had thus prevented an eventual change of some good subject who did good to the hospital.

The assistance of that hospital, I think, had been accepted shortly before my visit.

I do not know well whether to Mother Gattorno herself or to some other Superior I pointed out the inconveniences that could derive from having accepted the condition set out above, and it seems to me that it was promised me that provision would be made at the next expiry of the contract with the hospital administration.

I note that I never gave formal orders, nor made any decree in the course of my Apostolic Visitation; I only pointed out this or that inconvenience to the Superiors, reserving the right afterward to report everything to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, my mandate being ad referendum.

To hear it said that the Apostolic Visitation was in her Institute was for the Servant of God a great nightmare, from which she therefore sought to free herself, having recourse for this to the work of her Protectors, such as for example Cardinal Granito di Belmonte.

§ 310
The Servant of God demanded that the Sisters be treated well.

I seem to have heard it said that Mother Gattorno, discovering that in some house the Sisters suffered because of excessive economy, complained to the respective Superiors and protested, demanding that the Sisters be treated well. But under the table, through other Sisters, other invitations were made to send extraordinary gifts. So it seems to me. However, I do not believe that Mother Gattorno ever played a double part; indeed, of this I am sure.

The economic conditions of the Sisters in America were different from those in Italy, and those Sisters there certainly did not lack necessities.

§ 311
The deficiencies were attributed to the general system.

Asked to whom the Sisters imputed the lack of necessities for the Sisters themselves in some house, I answer that, being a true consequence of the general system, they did not impute it either to this one or to that one.

Here in Rome they were in need of money, and so it happened that some Superiors made their Sisters suffer, while others, however, thought above all that their Sisters must not lack necessities, and did not let them lack anything.

The simple Sisters, however, imputed it to the proximate cause, which practically and really was the true cause, that is, the local Superior.

§ 312
The Servant of God chose superiors well.

Asked whether Mother Gattorno was upright in the elections of the Provincial Superiors and of the Superiors of the large Houses of Rome and Piacenza, I must answer that I never came across Superiors who did not deserve to be in that post. Errors, naturally, can occur, but I could not say that she let herself be led by secondary ends.

§ 313
Prudent dispositions of the Servant of God before dying.

I am convinced that Mother Gattorno arranged justly and rightly, before dying, the economic part of the Institute and of her family.

And in fact, after her death no compromising documents for Mother Gattorno herself came to my knowledge. Only of importance, a little piece of paper was shown to me on which was written a cession of fifty thousand lire in favor of the family of her

p. 187

daughter; but while the signature was certainly Mother Gattorno's, the rest of the writing was in another hand. Which fact, together with the signature on the paper, could give rise to the suspicion of some fraud.

I know that afterward they had a long suit, with an outcome favorable to the Sisters. Certainly, her being a mother in the Civil Code did not favor the Sisters. Although the affection a mother owes to her children in whatever state she finds herself is certainly not to be reproved, yet the manifestation of this affection in Mother Gattorno seems to me to have exceeded the limits in her new condition as Foundress and Mother General of an Institute of Sisters. The adjacency of her daughter's House to that of the Sisters, both in Rome and in Piacenza, gave rise to the continual coming and going of the relatives, of which the Sisters complained, and I have grounds to believe that there was generosity in little gifts of food and perhaps also of other things on the part of the Sisters, I believe with the consent of Mother Gattorno.

§ 314
The son-in-law was the cause of much distress for the Servant of God.

I seem to have heard it said that, during Mother Gattorno's life, her son-in-law Barbiellini gave her much trouble, trying to wrest money or promises from her even by violent means, and that Mother Gattorno resisted.

I cannot speak of inconveniences of another kind in the relations of the said Barbiellini with the Sisters, nor did I ever have complaints about his moral conduct with the Sisters.

I noted that the Institute extended to too many aims and embraced missions too disparate; that for this reason they transcended a single formation, and also that the Novices were not much cared for in their spiritual formation.

I was also struck by the sight of a photograph that Mother Gattorno let herself be taken of almost as if inspired, while she was writing the rules, at least so I believe, that they were the rules. I cannot say, however, in particular, what advantages the Superiors who sent more extraordinary gifts of money to Mother Gattorno obtained.

Rt. Rev. Mgr. PIETRO PIACENZA

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: Knowing the Piacenza environment thoroughly, the witness is a good judge of the esteem prevailing around the Servant of God, and likewise of the relations she cultivated from the very beginnings of the foundation of the Daughters of St. Anne; here the Priest of the Mission Fr. His closeness to the Institute and his exhaustive acquaintance with Gattorno emerge from the information on its development and from the careful analysis of how she carried out the office of Superior General. Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1061, testis respondit:

§ 315
Particulars of the witness.

My name is Pietro Piacenza, son of the late Onorato and Teresa Crosignani. I was born at Castel San Giovanni, diocese of Piacenza, on 21 January 1847. I made my studies in the Episcopal Seminary of Piacenza and then in the Alberoni College of the same city. I was ordained priest on 18 September 1869; and a year and a half later I was made Chaplain of the Mother House of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza. I was then professor, first of belles-lettres, in the Seminary of Piacenza, and in 1878 I was made Archpriest and Vicar forane of Fiorenzuola d'Arda; in 1897 I was made Archpriest with care of souls in the Cathedral of Piacenza and at the same time Chaplain of the Daughters of St. Anne in their house for the Deaf-Mutes; and again professor in the Seminary, teaching ecclesiastical history and liturgy; and in 1904 I was appointed Apostolic Protonotary of the S. Congregation of Rites.

§ 316
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: Of Mother Rosa Gattorno I heard speak already from the time I was at the Alberoni College, where I had as my Confessor and

p. 189

professor Mr. Giambattista Tornatore, Lazarist, who was very well disposed toward the Servant of God and cooperated with her in the first foundation of the Institute.

He helped the Servant of God in drawing up the Rules, and there appears even outwardly in the collar of the Daughters of St. Anne a trace of his work, the same collar resembling perfectly that of the Lazarists.

Fr. Tornatore, even before his relation with M. Gattorno, was most devoted to St. Anne, Mother of the Most Holy Virgin: he had a life of her compiled by Mr. Cremisini, Superior of the Alberoni College, and inculcated devotion to her in everyone; he distributed images of her and I believe he influenced the increase of devotion in the spirit of the Servant of God.

The same Fr. Tornatore was also very devoted to the Ven. Clausi, propagated devotion to him, and inspired devotion to him in Mother Gattorno and her daughters. And to this is due the relation that followed between the Servant of God and the Paolotti, especially with their General Fr. Ricca, also a Genoese, and with Fr. Agostino Donadio, who frequented this generalate house until the last of his life and was present at the death of the Servant of God.

From the very first days that I was Chaplain of the Daughters of St. Anne in their Mother House of Piacenza, I knew the Servant of God, who was in that House bought by her from the Counts Del Verme (and it still keeps this name), and where she made Communion every day, and I myself administered it to her.

I note that in those times it was not the custom among Sisters to make Communion every day, not even among the Daughters of St. Anne themselves, who afterward, following the example of their Mother, made it ever more frequently, until making it daily.

§ 317
The witness's positive impression of the Servant of God.

And I can say from now that the manner in which she attended Holy Mass and all the other functions, and approached Holy Communion, made a most edifying impression on me.

I then always had contact with the Servant of God, also here in Rome, having had a few times occasion to say Mass in her presence and to administer Holy Communion to her: I always noted in her the same most edifying demeanor.

Besides personal acquaintance, I know her also through the relations she had with the Bishop of Piacenza, first Mgr. Ranza, then Mgr. Scalabrini, with Count Caracciolo, now deceased, and with Count Marazzani, likewise deceased, and with many of the secular and regular clergy.

Here I note that the persons most eminent for piety, of both clergies of Piacenza, all had a special relation with the Servant of God.

I recall Count Archdeacon Francesco Tedeschi, Count Vicedomo Giuseppe Gazzola, Canon Penitentiary Vincenzo Chiappini and Fr. Alessandro da Piacenza, Capuchin; Canon Provost of St. Antoninus, Don Domenico Costa, all deceased.
