I recall then that there always kept relations with the Servant of God and her daughters the living Archpriests Don Gaetano Bersani, Canon Don Francesco Armilunghi, still Chaplain of the Daughters of St. Anne, and Mgr. Camillo Mangot, who was Secretary to Mgr. Scalabrini, at present Provost of the Cathedral, as well as Mgr. Giovanni Battista Vinati, who was Vicar General of the Diocese, and now Bishop of Bosa in Sardinia.

All these had more or less great esteem for the virtue of the Servant of God, although perhaps not all esteem her worthy of the Altars.

These are my sources; I have no others of written things.

§ 318
Constant piety of the Servant of God and reputation for holiness.

Ad 8: What struck me in the Servant of God was the constancy in acts of piety and in the outward demeanor in those acts: and certainly this, in my opinion, must have contributed much to creating around her the esteem of a Saint.

I always had great esteem for her, but, as in many others of Piacenza and by name in the four Ecclesiastics named above and still living, my esteem does not reach the point of believing her worthy of the honors of the Altar.

I feel affection and veneration for her memory, and God grant that all difficulties be overcome for her to be beatified, but I have some fear.

Ad 9: I know that she was born at Genoa of a well-to-do family, but I know nothing of her childhood and adolescence. I know that she married and was left a widow with two children, one Alessandro, deceased, and the other a deaf-mute, still living and residing at Piacenza with Count Barbiellini her husband; but I do not know particulars.

p. 191

§ 319
Beginning of the foundation.

Ad 17: I have heard it said that even before the Servant of God went to Piacenza, having been left a widow, she had begun at Genoa itself to do something, united with other friends, especially with the sick in their homes. But induced afterward by the priest Cogrossi, a Cremonese, she went to Piacenza, where, having bought the Del Verme palace, she began to put into effect the foundation of her Institute.

Concerning this priest Cogrossi: he was the first priest the Servant of God had at Piacenza as her counselor. And at the beginning he lived in the same Del Verme palace. He enjoyed a reputation for great piety; he was elderly. The Servant of God already had with her other companions, some come with her from Genoa and others who joined at Piacenza.

On the other hand, the palace is very large and therefore his staying in that place could not give, and did not give, any handle to malicious tongues.

§ 320
Priests who collaborated in the foundation.

This priest Cogrossi enjoying a reputation for great piety, as I have said, Fr. Tornatore, who in his turn was very pious, desired to know him, and going several times to the Del Verme house, made his acquaintance and through him came to know the Servant of God also, with whom he then entered into the relation of which I have spoken above, becoming afterward her confessor and counselor.

When Cogrossi (I do not know whether also before) was called to Rome to the Holy Office, his relations with the Servant of God were broken off. It is to be excluded that Cogrossi was called to the Holy Office for reasons of morality, and I heard it said that he was called for his fanciful, visionary and exaggerated ideas.

I know that besides Fr. Tornatore, her principal counselor, the Servant of God made use also, for counsel, of the aforementioned Archdeacon Tedeschi, Canon Gazzola and Fr. Alessandro da Piacenza, Capuchin.

§ 321
First purpose of the Institute: care of the sick in their homes.

I recall that the first of the purposes set before the Daughters of St. Anne was established by the Servant of God in the care of the sick in their homes, and that Fr. Tornatore compiled for this service a special regulation in which, among other things, it was prescribed that the Sisters should always go in twos and that one should not leave the room without the other. The novelty of the thing and the rigidity of Fr. Tornatore demanded the most cautious precautions.

The Sisters from the beginning were much sought after, and never sufficed for the requests. And I must say that, having known seven or eight of the first Daughters of St. Anne, I esteemed them all as souls of great sacrifice and of extraordinary virtue.

§ 322
Fr. Tornatore, author of the first rules.

Ad 21, Proc. fol. 1070: I know that Fr. Tornatore wrote the rules for the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, and, going to his room in the Alberoni College when I was still a student, I saw, without however reading them, the writings, when he was occupied with them. I knew afterward that those writings were truly the rules, because he himself told me so. I know afterward that these rules are not the same as those approved by the Holy See, because of the dialogue form in which they were drawn up.

I know that Fr. Tornatore was very pleased that they should be called, and that he said: «They will be called "Daughters of St. Anne"».

I cannot know whether he was the only one to determine the name. I do not know, however, whether the Servant of God previously had the idea of another title.

Ad 22: She was the first Superior of the Institute, and always showed herself an intelligent mother to her daughters.

§ 323
Postulants were admitted with a certain ease.

As to receiving Postulants into her Institute, I must say first of all that the Servant of God received many requests for the opening of houses, and personnel was then always lacking to her. And therefore she was induced to admit with a certain ease. I recall that a young Piacenza schoolmistress, now deceased (I do not remember the name), called by the Sisters to teach in their house at Piacenza, was afterward urged, I know not by whom, to enter the Institute itself.

I was then very surprised to see her, a few months later, Superior in their house at Sampierdarena, and then to learn that she was transferred, always as Superior, to other houses. After about thirteen or fourteen years, and even more, she left the Institute and went to teach elementary school at Calendasco in the Piacenza area, where, as I know from the parish priest of that place, Don Egidio Agazzini, she showed much animosity toward the Institute she had left, and deplored having entered it, and added that truly she had never felt attraction for the religious state. So great was the animosity that she had also drifted from practices of piety, and returned to them only in the last month of her life at the urging of the parish priest. I must note that when she left the Institute this Sister was no longer Superior, and I never heard anything said against her moral conduct.

p. 193

I know of another young Emilian schoolmistress (whose name likewise I do not recall) who, a few months after she had taken the religious habit, was sent as Superior to a new house of theirs in Piacenza, where there were some eighty girls who worked at the loom, and who after two or three years left the Institute.

I know that Bishop Mgr. Scalabrini did not approve this ease in accepting Postulants and then sending them as Superiors. These things happened in the first decade of the foundation.

I can add further that a certain Sister Tornatore, sister of Mr. Tornatore, Lazarist, left another religious Institute to enter that of the Daughters of St. Anne, and that two other nieces of the same Mr. Tornatore also entered this Institute, and that (it seems to me) the elder of these two, Sr. Anna Giuseppina, once said with me: «This Institute has sprung up like pumpkins, which quickly grow and then wither». If Sr. Anna Giuseppina did not say it to me, it will have been another Sister of good spirit.

I cannot say what precautions the Servant of God used in the admissions and in the assignment of Superiors.

§ 324
She watched over the observance of the rules and preceded all by example.

As far as I know, it is certain that the Servant of God watched over the observance of the rules of her Institute and preceded all by example.

The Sisters lived at the beginning in financial straits; in food they had to make do as best they could. And to the Sisters from my parts, there being no such custom, the use of pumpkin flowers as a dish made a somewhat bad impression. I know that the Servant of God took great care of the sick Sisters.

§ 325
Too much communication at Piacenza between the mother's house and the daughter's.

Ad 23: It made a great impression on me to see that in the mother house at Piacenza there was an internal communication, on the side of the garden, with the house of her daughter, married to Count Barbiellini, and that the nurse with the children was frequently seen in the courtyard and in the corridors of the Sisters; and to see the Sisters themselves with the Servant of God's little grandchildren in their arms. And this thing made an impression not only on me, but also on other priests, and much more on Mgr. Scalabrini, who said: «It is absolutely necessary that that communicating door be closed»; and added that he had said so many times also to the Servant of God. And two or three years after Mgr. Scalabrini told me this, a Visitor had it closed, I think about '82 or '83. And I saw it closed. The coming and going of the family of the Servant of God's daughter did not give rise to dishonoring gossip. The Servant of God entrusted the execution of many things to her son-in-law Count Gaspare Barbiellini, and it was said, I do not know with what foundation, that he lived at the expense of the Servant of God, who, however, had money at her disposal.

From the knowledge I have of the Servant of God, I cannot sup-

§ 326
The Servant of God's relations with her family: her son Alessandro.

pose that she touched, to the advantage of the family, a single cent belonging to the Institute. Count Barbiellini also had the charge of purveyor of the Piacenza house and therefore entered the Sisters' kitchen, the refectory, not however when the Sisters were at table, and other places where not even I ever entered. The Servant of God also had a son, by the name of Alessandro, who was by temperament somewhat scatterbrained.

The Servant of God tried to put him in good hands, and when he was fifteen or sixteen she entrusted him to Don Gaetano Bersani, an excellent priest and capable of guiding the son well; he kept him with himself in his house, the Servant of God paying him the board. Grown to adulthood, after an absence whose length I do not recall, the Servant of God entrusted to him the management of the estate called Gargatano, given to her by Count Francesco Caracciolo. Alessandro went there to cohabit with a woman, whom some suspected was not his wife; but I exclude this suspicion, because the Servant of God would never have permitted such cohabitation. I know that this son afterward made a very edifying death.

Ad 25, Proc. fol. 1076v.: Of the Apostolic Visitation I know nothing. I know, however, something of another visit. When I was Archpriest at Fiorenzuola, about 1884, there withdrew to live there a certain Giovannina Schenardi, of that same town, who had left the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. She always behaved well from the time I knew her, and now she takes to the normal schools the boarders whom the Gianelline Sisters of Piacenza keep. Before leaving the Institute she was Superior in the house at Orbetello, and told me that she had been sent away from the Institute, with another companion of hers, because she had not obeyed an order that had come to her from the Generalate

p. 195

House to make two Sisters leave, because a Visitor was arriving at that house.

I have heard it said that one of the Cardinal Protectors sometimes sent someone to visit this or that house for his own particular reasons; I could not say, however, whether this was one of the cases.

Schenardi added that she had naturally refused and was therefore sent away. I did not see the letter by which it was imposed to make those Sisters suffer. Schenardi showed me a letter from the Vicar of Orbetello, another from a Bishop of a city where she had been Superior, and another, I do not know whether from the Cardinal Prefect or Secretary, or from another official of a Roman Congregation: in which letters she was declared right. I do not recall, however, that the matter on which she was declared right was explained there.

§ 327
The Servant of God, model of Christian and religious life.

Ad 26: I not only believe that the Servant of God faithfully observed the commandments of God, the precepts of the Church and the obligations of her own state, but rather that she was always a model, both in the world, although I did not then know her, and when she was a religious.

§ 328
She practiced the virtues in an eminent manner.

Ad 27: By induction, from the facts I have known of the Servant of God, I hold that she possessed and practiced the three Theological Virtues, the four Cardinal ones, and all the others connected, such as humility, poverty, chastity, obedience. I deduce that she possessed faith in a very lively way, from the way in which she practiced acts of piety; for example: meditation, which she always made kneeling, while to some Sisters she sometimes said: «Sit down», and Communion, and to do the one and the other she employed an hour and a half, and I saw her spend it always kneeling. I do not know whether in the last years of her life she sat while making meditation. I had occasion to note it, because I went to celebrate Mass in the Sisters' house early and stayed some time in the Sisters' house, and I always confessed to Mr. Tornatore, who was always there.

§ 329
Constant and edifying prayer of the Servant of God.

Teaching singing to the girls of that house, and going to hear the confessions of the girls not yet admitted to Holy Communion, and moreover going to give Benediction with the Most Blessed Sacrament almost every evening, I had occasion to see the Servant of God often in the Church praying, and the constant and edifying manner in which she made the visit to the Most Blessed Sacrament in the afternoon hours, and I noted that it was rather long and always kneeling. The Servant of God, in agreement with Mr. Tornatore, on whose counsel she always proceeded, established that exposition of the Most Blessed Sacrament be often held in the Chapel of that Mother House. I recall that the Servant of God went to adoration in the most inconvenient hours, and when the other Sisters could not because of their duties, and she went also in the time when the Sisters took a little recreation.

§ 330
Most devoted to the Eternal Father and to the Passion; other devotions.

Altogether, in those days, at the exposition she remained several hours. The Servant of God was most devoted to the Eternal Father. I do not know whether she had such devotion already before her relations with Mr. Tornatore. If she did not have it, it was instilled in her by this Religious, who had it in the highest degree; and she wanted the month of January consecrated to the Eternal Father, and I went every evening to give the benediction and read each evening a special prayer written by Fr. Tornatore.

Most devoted she was also to the Crucified and to the Passion of Our Lord.

Being charged to preach the sermon on the Passion a few days before Good Friday, in place of another who could no longer come, as I recited that discourse she was so moved that she burst into loud and copious weeping, so that I too was moved, and my emotion was then communicated to the whole audience, so that, through the devotion of the Servant of God, my discourse, composed in such haste, proved of profit to all.

The letters she wrote she marked with these three initials A.M.F., to indicate St. Anne, Our Lady, St. Francis of Assisi.

To nourish piety in her Sisters and to instruct them, besides the Conferences that Mr. Tornatore often gave, besides the spiritual exercises that she had given them, she often invited some Religious, and more frequently I remember a Jesuit, a Capuchin, a Discalced Carmelite, to give some sermon.

I cannot specify anything of extraordinary facts regarding her devotion to Our Lady, although I am persuaded that she had it most tender.

Her devotion to St. Anne appears evident from the name given to her Institute and from the month of July, which she wanted consecrated to her. I recall that in this month in the morning after Mass the month

p. 197

of the Most Precious Blood was held, in the evening that of St. Anne, and I gave the benediction, in both the one and the other.

Of the images of St. Anne that she had made in oil for the Church of the Mother House, she had thousands and thousands of copies reproduced in print, and continued always throughout her life to send copies here and there to propagate the devotion. To her Sisters she wished to give, besides the distinctive name, the common name of Anna.

Of St. Francis of Assisi the novena was made in that house. In honor of St. Joseph she wanted the month of March consecrated in that Mother House, which in Piacenza was not yet general, and he had not yet been proclaimed by Pius IX Patron of the universal Church.

She was devoted also to St. Francis of Paola, and perhaps it was a consequence of the devotion to the Ven. Clausi, inoculated in her by Mr. Tornatore. In the Chapel of the Mother House, I remember, the Servant of God had had the image of this Saint affixed. She was devoted likewise to St. Michael the Archangel and had his feast celebrated with solemnity. Both to Mgr. Ranza and to Mgr. Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, the Servant of God always showed herself most deferential; and these Bishops were in their turn deferential to the Servant of God. And Mgr. Scalabrini, for St. Anne, not only went to celebrate in their Chapel, but also accepted the invitation to dinner and even stayed as a guest in this house when he came to Rome. It is to be noted then that the Bishop, on the said feast, preferred to go and celebrate in the Chapel of the Daughters of St. Anne than to go to the Parish of St. Anne of that same city! The parish priest complained and the Bishop said: «But what can I do? In that house so much good is done»; and I heard him many times praise Mother Gattorno.

§ 331
Her charity toward her neighbor was excellent.

Proc. fol. 1126: As to the charity of the Servant of God toward the Lord, I refer to what I have already said concerning the virtue of faith.

As to charity toward the neighbor, the very purpose of the foundation of her Institute already says it, for the sick, principally poor, in their homes. Then she took into the Mother House more than fifty girls taken off the street.

I learned that she took an interest in our Italians when they occupied Eritrea, and sent some of her Sisters there, and there she took in little African girls.

I still remember the first expedition that the Servant of God made of her Sisters to America; and I know that afterward they spread greatly there. And all the foundations of the Servant of God have this aim: to do spiritual and temporal good to souls; and in this she did not seek material advantages for her Institute. Rather I recall that in I no longer know which hospital, but it seems to me in Emilia, an Institute of Sisters was being sought, but with none could they manage to come to terms because of the modest resources at its disposal.

This fact reached the ear of the Servant of God, and she promptly offered the work of her Institute, which was accepted. Following this fact three other hospitals, those of Borgo San Donnino, of Fiorenzuola and of Corte Maggiore, also wanted the Daughters of St. Anne, whereas before they had never thought of Sisters because of the difficulty of the expense; and they are still there.

§ 332
She cared for the sick out of charity.

To come better to the aid of the poor sick, she saw to it that her Sisters should learn to perfection the art of caring for them, and therefore she had two certified nurses come from Turin to Piacenza, in order to teach her Sisters.

For her Sisters she provided a health house on the estate of Gargatano which, as we have said, was given to her, and she wanted them to have a Chaplain at their disposal, since it was far from the Parish.

In this connection it comes to my mind that there was a little friction, because the parish priest would have liked to take charge exclusively of that house; but then things were settled, especially through the care of the present Bishop of Piacenza. I know that there was some complaint at times about the doctor's care, but I consider such complaints unjustified; it may be, it is true, that sometimes the doctor of that rural district was occupied with other patients, and prevented from hastening promptly at the Sisters' call, but this could happen in any place. And in any case it does not seem to me that the Servant of God, in placing the health house there for her Sisters, acted lightly, all the more so since I know that sick Genoese come by tradition to seek health on the banks of the Po in the Piacenza area.

I recall that there was at Piacenza a certain Count, whose name may I be allowed to keep silent, a great admirer of the Servant of God, and also

p. 199

a benefactor of her works; who, however, did not practice his Christian faith at all, and I know for certain that he did not make his Easter duty. Having been abandoned by his wife, he had put into the house a governess for two little daughters of his who had been left in tender age; and rumors little favorable ran about him. The Servant of God, little by little, induced him to dismiss the governess, and then to frequent the Sacraments; and I gave this Gentleman Communion many times in the Sisters' chapel. He then continued in this manner of life until death.

As to Prudence, I know that from the beginning she did nothing without the counsel principally of Fr. Tornatore. I know also that she turned to other authoritative persons for counsel, among them a certain Fr. Alessandro da Piacenza, Capuchin, much esteemed and appreciated and sought after for his prudence in counsels, and now deceased. The Servant of God often sent for him, all the more since the Capuchins' garden bordered on the Sisters' garden, and I myself sometimes went to call him on the Servant of God's commission.

I do not know, further, that she accepted anything lightly.

§ 334
She showed herself very grateful toward benefactors.

I cannot relate specific facts of the virtue of Justice of the Servant of God because I do not know them. It results to me, however, from my own personal experience, that the Servant of God felt gratitude greatly and showed it in the best way she could. Not being able to compensate me in money, she wanted me to go and relax a little at Sampierdarena, in Genoa, where I had never been; and she had the Sisters launder, iron and sew my linen, and they showed me every attention even when I was not in her houses as chaplain, and, when I came to Rome, she lodged me in her house.

§ 335
Of impulsive nature, she knew how to control herself well.

As to temperance, I have heard it said that the Servant of God was of an impulsive nature; but I never noticed it; and the Sisters who told me this added that she did not let herself be overcome; I always found her gentle and even.

As to external mortification, I know that she not only never ate meat, but could not even eat foods that had been cooked in vessels in which there had been broth or something else fatty. And I recall that when she came to Fiorenzuola, seeing that the Sisters had brought vessels for the kitchen, and I having remarked to them that they were useless, it was answered me that they were exclusively for their Mother, for whom it would have been impossible to eat foods cooked in other vessels that had served for fatty foods. And I having observed to Fr. Tornatore that this not being able to bear even a distant taste of fatty foods seemed to me a little excessive, he answered me: «I believe she does it so that even the taste of meat may no longer come to her mind».

I must note that, although I found myself many times eating with the Sisters, alone or with other guests, I never saw her taste or drink anything.

§ 336
She was humble, modest and a lover of chastity.

Proc. fol. 1140: As I am persuaded that the Servant of God possessed the Theological and Cardinal virtues, so also I hold that the virtue of humility was not lacking to her, from the impressions I carried away of her in conversing with her, and I never noticed that she failed against this virtue.

As to external acts of hers in which this virtue truly shone, either I did not know them or at least for now they do not come to my mind.

The demeanor of the Servant of God and her modesty of the eyes were such that they made one immediately notice her great love of the beautiful virtue. And from some incident I perceived how much she loved this virtue, and she wanted her Sisters to abstain from any familiarity, even the most innocent, with Ecclesiastics, and from conversing with them without necessity.

§ 337
She obeyed superiors blindly.

As to obedience, I would have nothing to the contrary to say, but one thing made an impression on me: her delaying the closing of the communicating door with her daughter's garden at Piacenza, although Monsignor Scalabrini (so at least he told me) had told her many times to close it. I do not know, however, whether he ever gave her such an order during the short time in which he was Protector of the Institute. Apart from this fact I would have nothing else to say that is unfavorable to her virtue of obedience. Indeed I must say that toward Fr. Tornatore she exercised the most blind obedience.

I know that she had veneration for any Ecclesiastic; and, for the respect she had for them, she wished that they too would seek to dress in a manner befitting their dignity. I say this because I was once present when the Servant of God, speaking

p. 201

§ 338
She practiced the virtues constantly to a heroic degree.

to a certain Don Accinelli, who in Genoa administered her affairs, seeing him a little slovenly in dress, said: «But dear Don Accinelli, it is fitting that you dress more neatly, to command that respect due to your character».

I can say with complete certainty that the Servant of God was always constant in the exercise of these virtues until death; but I could not say to what degree she reached in the practice of the said virtues! Certain it is that, taken as a whole, she practiced them in an uncommon degree.

Ad 30: As to extraordinary gifts of the Servant of God, there comes to my mind this fact, which made a certain impression on me.

§ 339
Extraordinary gifts in the life of the Servant of God.

I was already Archpriest of Fiorenzuola when in Piacenza the influenza epidemic broke out among the children; and the Servant of God, alarmed at the danger her two little grandchildren were running, sent for me and, when I was with her, asked me to find for her, and at once, a house suitable for her and two or three other Sisters and for her two little grandchildren at Fiorenzuola. I note that it was summer and that the Servant of God too would have needed a little country air, and she did not yet at that time have the Gargatano house at their disposal. At the request of the Servant of God I was somewhat dismayed, because I did not know how to provide at once for her desire.

But the Servant of God, dismissing me, said to me with an accent of conviction: «Go, go, I shall pray and you will find». Having left the Servant of God, after a few steps I met a parishioner of mine, a certain Foroni, now deceased (I do not remember the name), and I took advantage of this meeting to explain to him my embarrassment at having been given the task of finding at once a suitable house for religious in my parish, and he answered me: «But if you wish, I can give you my house near the Oratory of Gallo; which is two hundred meters from Fiorenzuola on the Roman road». I was amazed, because it was exactly what was needed, and I had not thought of it at all until then. Add that, given the urgency of the Servant of God's request, it was wonderful that Mr. Foroni also should be in Piacenza that very day, and that I should meet him not far from the Sisters' house, so that I could at once bring the happy news to the Servant of God.

§ 340
Reputation for holiness.

Ad 38: Concerning the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God, I can say that in Piacenza, although she was much esteemed during life, and also after death, even as a Holy Sister, yet among the Clergy of that City this esteem does not reach the point of believing her worthy of the honor of the Altars.

WITNESS VIII
Sr. ANNA SANTINA SOLENGHI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 131 of 26 April 1915 (fol. 1161v.) to Sess. 146[...] of 5 June 1915 (fol. 1288v.).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Superior of the Generalate House, Assistant General.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she met the Servant of God: 19 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness met her: 36 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 67 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness met the Servant of God in June 1867, when she asked to be admitted into the Institute; they therefore lived together for long periods, and only the death of the Foundress, which occurred on 6 May 1900, interrupted the intimate familiarity.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The witness entered the Institute a year after the foundation, knew the family of the Servant of God, was uninterruptedly a superior from 1872 and Assistant General from 1888 and therefore in very close contact with the Foundress. All this means that the witness acquired of the Servant of God a deep knowledge which, however, shuns easy enthusiasms. A deposition of great importance results: objective, serene and extremely circumstantial. The subject of the virtues, in particular, is very extensive and detailed — so much so that we found ourselves led to abbreviate it — with objective and valid elements of judgment. The subject of the reputation for holiness is also treated with ample information and direct knowledge of it.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1164v., testis respondit:

§ 341
Particulars of the witness.

My name is Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi; I was born at Agazzano (Province and Diocese of Piacenza) on 24 April 1848, of the late Giuseppe and Francesca Codeini. I was brought up in the Christian faith by my parents, and at about ten I was admitted to first Communion. From childhood I heard Holy Mass every day, and from my earliest years I had the habit of receiving Communion frequently, and since I have been a Religious I approach every day to receive the Eucharist, and I go to confession every week. I entered this Institute on 3 November 1867 at Piacenza and was received by the Servant of God, Rosa Gattorno. I took the habit on Shrove Thursday of 1868, and I do not remember well how long afterward I made religious profession. In 1872 I was made Superior of the house of Genoa, where I had already been Vice-Superior before. In the first Chapter held in the Institute (I do not remember the year) I was made Assistant General, and I have always remained Assistant General; and together with this I was then local Superior of our House in Vicolo Margana in Rome, then of that of Florence and then of this Generalate House of Rome, except for a short time in which I was sent back as Superior to Genoa.

§ 342
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 8: I met the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno when I presented myself to her, I do not know well whether at Pentecost or at Corpus Domini of the year 1867, asking to be received into her Institute.

Before that I had not heard of her, and I presented myself to the Servant of God on the advice of the Gentlemen of the Mission of Piacenza, who had come to Gragnano, where I was at the time, to preach, and to whom I had expressed my desire to become a Religious. When I presented myself to the Servant of God for the first time she was still dressed as a lay person, but she took the habit on the feast of St. Anne of that same year; so that when I entered the Institute afterward, I found her in the religious habit.

I was much in contact with the Servant of God, indeed always with her during my stay in Rome, which began, as I have said, in 1877 and was interrupted for nine years by the office of Superior that I held in the House of Florence. But also in this house of Florence I had frequent occasion to see and speak with the Servant of God. I often saw her again during my stay in Genoa, because the Servant of God, being young and full of activity, often made herself seen in the houses.

§ 343
Birth and relations of the Servant of God with her family.

Ad 9: My memory does not serve me much and I could not determine many dates. In any case, I shall say that when she died fifteen years ago she was sixty-nine years old. From this one can work back to the year of her birth, which took place in Genoa, of a most pious mother, but of a father who certainly did not want to know much about Religion. I do not know, however, how far he aimed in matters of religiosity or irreligiosity. Her parents were well-off, and her father was a man of business. Of the Servant of God there still live two sisters in Genoa (provided that none has died in these days): Elisa, a most pious Lady, and Giusta, so-so. She also had a half-sister by the name of Giggia, a most pious Lady, since her mother had had another husband before Gattorno. I do not know whether she had other sisters: she had three brothers, Federico, Francesco and Emanuele, who died many years ago. Federico died two years ago. All three, however, were not at all Religious.

Ad 10: I know from her brothers that they were very fond of the Servant of God from the time she was a child, and especially Federico, who was crazy about his Nina, the diminutive by which they called her in the family. And this makes me believe that she was from childhood very good. Her mother, then, Adelaide, whom I knew very well and whom I also assisted in her illness, always spoke well to me of her Nina, and said she was very fond of her precisely for her goodness, from the time she was a child. I also knew well the father of the Servant of God, I spoke with him many times in Genoa, and he too always told me much good of his Nina. And her sisters too spoke of her to me with affection and esteem.

In the Institute I then heard of the youth of the Servant of God as of an excellent young woman and a model wife and widow.

Ad 11: I heard it said in the Institute that the Servant of God would not have wanted to hear of marriage, but that she was compelled by her parents. This husband was a certain Custo, and I could say nothing else. The Servant of God never spoke to me of it.

Ad 16: Her son Alessandro died at thirty-five, and the Servant of God exerted herself greatly that he might die as a Christian, since she had not been able to obtain, to her great tribulation, that he live as a Christian. I too took part in assisting the son in his last illness; the Servant of God assisted him in the last month and, resigned in a Christian manner, bore the loss.

§ 344
After her husband's death she gave herself to piety and charity.

After the death of her husband, the Servant of God gave herself wholly to works of piety and charity. She visited the sick in the hospital of Pammatone, and was directress of the Daughters of Mary, by commission of the Archbishop. I recall that the Servant of God, speaking of that time of her widowhood, often named Frassinetti, Prior of Santa Sabina, of whom she spoke with great esteem; but I cannot specify why she named him, though it seems to me it was in connection with the Daughters of Mary, with whom Frassinetti was concerned. I know that with the Sisters the Servant of God often spoke of a certain Capuchin lay Brother of Camporosso, who died with a reputation for holiness, who foretold her various things, and especially sufferings. She had great trust in him and consulted him often when she was in the world. I heard the Servant of God say that she was much occupied with the Daughters of Mary, of whom she was directress, and gave them conferences.

§ 345
Foundation of the Institute and relations with Fr. Tornatore.

Ad 17: When the Servant of God went to Piacenza, she wanted to found the Institute of the Daughters of the Immaculate, and for this reason, when I entered, I found a draft of rules for the Daughters of the Immaculate, and on the high altar of the Chapel there was the image of the Immaculate, while that of St. Anne stood on a side altar. When I entered, however, the change of name to Daughters of St. Anne had already taken place, and I believe it occurred through the influence of Fr. Tornatore, of the Gentlemen of the Mission, of whom the Servant of God went to ask the direction for her Institute in the early times when she was at Piacenza, and Fr. Tornatore was most devoted to St. Anne.

I recall that Fr. Tornatore told me, I think in this very generalate house, that before knowing the Servant of God he had a dream in which he saw many Ladies in procession, among whom he saw one who led them, and that when the Servant of God presented herself to him at the Alberoni College, he recognized precisely that she was the one he had seen in that dream leading that procession of Ladies. Fr. Tornatore then concluded: «Your Mother is a Saint».

Proc. fol. 1174v.: Fr. Tornatore, of whom I spoke in the preceding session, was regarded as a father by our Sisters, as if he were a co-founder. He always esteemed the Servant of God greatly. He ceased to assist the Institute about 1889, and the reasons why he left the Institute I could not say. I remember well that to the last he exhorted the Sisters to obey and to abide by what the Servant of God said. He drew up our rules, as he himself told me, but I do not know then whether they are the same as those approved by the Holy See. He greatly helped the Institute by procuring for it Mass stipends for the Chaplains who came to our Houses, and by obtaining for it other gifts from respectable families.

§ 346
Pius IX and the foundation of the Institute.

Ad 18: I heard from the very mouth of the Servant of God that Pius IX contributed with his counsel to the foundation of the Institute, exhorting her to set her hand to the work while she still felt reluctant, and that the same Pius IX told her that her Institute would then spread most rapidly.

§ 347
Financial straits in the early days of the foundation.

Ad 20: In the first times of the foundation the Institute found itself in financial straits, and the Servant of God, to maintain the Sisters, had recourse also to the sale of precious objects of her family, for which she afterward gave compensation. Because of the financial straits of the early times there was not much on our table, but nonetheless in one way or another we managed to satisfy our hunger. Recourse was sometimes had also to cornbread, and for supper sometimes to only cooked apples with a little sugar, and bread.

I remember it well, because I too was there in those times. At noon, in those times, there was soup and a single dish. The Sisters, however, were all content, and one sees that the Lord wanted this Institute, giving them the spirit necessary to overcome these difficulties. The Lord made subjects from excellent and most distinguished families arrive at the Institute in the early times, showing by this too that He wanted the work, and blessed it.

§ 348
Religious fervor at the beginning of the foundation.

Among these distinguished elements I remember well Sr. Anna Francesca Camisa and Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino. The Servant of God welcomed into her Institute women who were rather elderly, but full of fervor, and who nourished especially a great devotion to St. Anne. I recall in particular some little old women of Cortemaggiore and of other places, in whom Fr. Tornatore had instilled a great devotion to St. Anne, and who, having entered the Institute, edified me greatly by their singular fervor. When I entered the Institute I found the habit as we wear it now, except that, for reasons of economy, the veil we wear on the head was smaller; and in winter a little woolen jacket was worn, but this lasted only a very short time. I believe the idea of our habit comes from our Foundress. The Servant of God did not at once put on the religious habit when her first companions took it, and she waited almost a year. I could not say the reason for this delay, but I know, however, that in that time she traveled much to beg alms in aid of her Institute, and to find young women who would follow her in her Institute.

Ad 21: The rules we have at present were approved; and Cardinal Verga, Protector of the Institute, brought the Servant of God the approval of them on the occasion of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the foundation of the Institute.

Ad 22: The first Superior General of our Institute was the Servant of God. I exclude that she was ever in that post out of vanity.

§ 349
A certain ease in the acceptance of postulants.

After the approval of the rules, in the acceptance of Postulants and in the Novitiate they were perfectly adhered to; but before, the Servant of God accepted the young girls, whether or not they had a dowry, whether they were more or less than twenty-five; yet I could not at all say that she lacked prudence in the acceptance and the necessary precautions. The Servant of God was pressed by the requests for foundations of houses, and needed a great deal of personnel. I heard from priests, I do not remember which, and I exclude Fr. Tornatore and Fr. Agostino Donadio, that sometimes a reproach was made to the Servant of God that she was hasty in accepting Postulants and in opening new houses; but I myself so liked this accepting with a certain breadth both Postulants and new houses that, when the Servant of God asked my opinion, I encouraged her to accept both Postulants and new houses. When afterward the Servant of God perceived, in that little Novitiate that she had those who came make in the early times, and also afterward, that the newcomers did not have the spirit necessary for the Institute, she did not hesitate to send them home; and after, with the approval of the rule, the novitiates were constituted according to canonical forms, it was easier to know them before profession and so send them home. I must note that, before the approval of the rules, although the Novices were soon clothed and sent here and there according to the needs of the Institute, it was nonetheless not permitted that they make vows before they had completed a year of probation.

§ 350
The Servant of God took counsel in the affairs of the Institute.
§ 351
Most active, but always vigilant over the observance of the rule.

When the Servant of God had some extraordinary matter in hand, she called her Assistants to counsel, and I too was sometimes consulted when I was in Florence. And much more she consulted her assistants when they were around her. I recall that votes were taken on the proposals that were made. Minutes were drawn up and we approved the forms. The Servant of God often visited the houses of her Institute, and with great diligence, and often with much sacrifice. I recall one time that, having arrived in Genoa, when I was there, not feeling well because of a pleurisy recently had, she applied a blister plaster, and the next morning tore it off and, having put a little cotton in the place of the plaster, set off to visit the houses. She was most active and most solicitous that regular discipline be observed. She recommended prayer and the manner of conducting oneself with the sick (the principal purpose of the Institute). She recommended to us that we never remain alone in caring for the sick, so that one would serve as guard to the other. And these recommendations she made to us always to the last, and when she could not, because of infirmities and years, go visiting the houses, she made use now of this now of that Sister to send them visiting the various houses. And I recall that I too, when I was in Florence, was called by telegram and sent twice on visitation. She did not, however, always make use of the same person, but according as seemed to her most opportune. To those she sent she recommended that they make a precise and exact report of the visit made.

§ 352
No partiality in the choice of persons: the case of Sorrentino.

In choosing personnel for the offices and posts of the Institute, the Servant of God did not let herself be carried away by secondary ends nor by particular personalities, but chose according as she believed most opportune and suitable.

There were rumors of partiality because of the attitude of the Servant of God toward Mother Teresa Sorrentino, because from the Novitiate she had a certain familiarity with her, then because she elected her Assistant General rather soon, then also because she sent her to Palermo, her native city, where she allowed her to open a house only for young noble girls, whereas we are instituted principally for the poorer classes.

But against such rumors I declare that it seems to me there is nothing to condemn in the Servant of God:

First, because Sorrentino is above all a religious of excellent spirit;

p. 209

Second, because, coming to this Novitiate at great sacrifice to herself, the Servant of God had to take account of her special condition;

Third, Sorrentino's intelligence and life, joined with her excellent religious spirit, were more than sufficient title to the office of Assistant General;

Fourth, in Palermo, where she was sent, by her social condition she could do greater good than elsewhere, and

Fifth, more in the upper class than in the poor class, because of her relations in that same class.

§ 353
The case of Chifenti and Card. Verga.

Proc. fol. 1184v.: There were other rumors against the Servant of God, because they said that Sr. Anna Francesca Chifenti had been clothed too soon, and admitted too soon to the Secretariat: which aroused jealousies in others, such as Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza. Before entering the Institute, this Sister studied singing in our school at Florence, when I was its Superior, and had a fine voice, and it was said that the Servant of God had so soon promoted her out of sympathy. To me too it seems that the Servant of God would have done better to test this Sister Anna Francesca in a rigorous Novitiate a little longer, whereas, on the contrary, after a very short time (I do not remember, but this occurred before the approval of the Rules) she admitted her to the General Secretariat, while she was still part of the Novitiate, of which therefore she could not follow all the practices and the discipline. Sr. Anna Francesca was very skillful and charming in her ways; she was intelligent, capable of carrying out activity in the Secretariat; and the Servant of God (so the others of the Secretariat told me) always had, so to speak, Checca on her lips and called her first in everything. I do not remember when she made profession.

As I said, the Servant of God always made use of this Sister, and put her in so many good relations with Cardinal Verga that he in the end appreciated her more than the other Sisters of the Secretariat and than the Servant of God herself.

The Cardinal began to come to this house very often and for some time even every day. He stayed sometimes to dinner with the Sisters of the Secretariat and sometimes even had supper and slept here, and after supper a little recreation was held with him. It was noticed that he always directed the conversation to Sr. A. Francesca, and I too observed it; sometimes in the garden he stayed alone with the same Sister, and all this gave rise to no little gossip, to the point of its being said that the Cardinal did not come here for the Servant of God, but for Sr. Anna Francesca. Having heard this gossip, I thought it my duty to go one morning to the Cardinal and warn him. After this, Sr. Anna Francesca gave me certain digs and addressed certain words to me, from which I formed the conviction that the Cardinal had revealed to her, wholly or in part, my filial warning. Then I decided to take no further interest. The Servant of God too noticed the Cardinal's attitude toward Sr. Anna Francesca, and hers toward the Cardinal, and learned that even in the house it had been said that the Cardinal, in the new Chapter, would make Sr. Anna Francesca General. I do not believe that the Servant of God was moved by any ambition to remain in the post of General, but naturally she desired the progress in spirit of the Institute she had founded, and with us, Assistant Sisters and Superiors who already knew the matters, she complained of the Cardinal's conduct with Sr. Anna Francesca. Before the Cardinal the Servant of God behaved politely, but after these events she began to be more reserved before him. The Cardinal began to thin out his visits. The Servant of God, taking occasion of an illness of Sr. Anna Francesca, sent her to Naples to be treated, entrusting her at the same time with the office of Secretary to a Superior of our house of the hospital of the Pace.

After having been several years in Naples, Sr. A. Francesca abandoned the Institute and married, and I believe she is now in Florence; I know, however, that she leads a good life and sometimes has even written to me.

§ 354
Prudent government of the Servant of God.

After Sr. A. Francesca's departure from Rome, the Cardinal thinned out his visits to this house still further, and a mutual coldness arose between us and him. I must say, however, that the Servant of God always showed herself polite and submissive to him. In the visitations that she made, the Servant of God provided as she judged opportune, with changes also of personnel, not excluding the Superiors, and often took immediate measures. She looked even at the smallest things concerning the observance of the rules, gathered the most minute information, also outside the visitations, and these measures she always took with rectitude of intention. She did not want the necessary to be lacking in the houses, while wanting, however, that all possible economies be made. She saw to it that sick Sisters were well cared for.

Ad 23: The Servant of God prescribed that the houses dependent on the Generalate should send to it every six months their surplus.

§ 355
Solicitude of the Servant of God for her deaf-mute daughter.

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 1191: The Servant of God tried to treat her deaf-mute daughter physically also, so that she might hear, but after many expenses it was found that everything was useless. After withdrawing her from the Institute for the deaf-mutes of Milan, the Servant of God always kept her daughter Carlotta with her, taking her on some rare occasions from Piacenza to Genoa or elsewhere.

As long as this Carlotta was unmarried, she always stayed with us, and we gladly put up with it because she was the daughter of our mother. As she grew older, however, she desired a husband, whereas the Servant of God would rather have wished very much that she become a nun; just as she herself would have wished very much that her son Alessandro had become a priest. Carlotta then became a bit capricious. I do not know, however, that she did foolish things on that account. The Servant of God having once entrusted her to the Countess or Marchioness Celoni, one evening, I think precisely in the house of that same Lady, on the occasion of a ball, Miss Carlotta met Count Gaspare Amidei-Barbiellini, with whom the marriage was afterward concluded, with the consent of the Servant of God, I think in 1876, and was celebrated in Genoa, in the house of Mrs. Adelaide, the mother of the Servant of God. Their honeymoon was at Lourdes; but, I do not know why, after only a very few days from their departure I saw them turn up at my house in Genoa, where I then was Superior, already back. Carlotta was very fond of her husband, but could not be without her mamma, and this is why, both in Rome and in Piacenza, the house near ours was built or bought. On the other hand, the Servant of God too, who always suffered for this daughter all her life, wanted her always near.

§ 356
Relations of the Servant of God with her son-in-law Barbiellini.

In Piacenza, after the purchase of the house, the Servant of God wished to build a wing for the Novitiate and at the same time Count Barbiellini also had his house enlarged a little. This gentleman then directed the works and took care of paying the workmen. Since the Servant of God had great trust in her son-in-law, it was said that the son-in-law took advantage precisely of this esteem to deceive his mother-in-law, making her pay the construction expenses of both our Novitiate and the enlargement of his house, making the expenses of both appear as due for his construction. The present Superior of Piacenza, Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni, I believe could say something about this.

Between our house and that of the daughter an internal communication was then opened, which afterward, I do not know how long after, was ordered closed, and I remember well, before the mother died, and if I am not mistaken it was ordered closed by the Apostolic Visitor, the living Cardinal Serafini.

I know for certain that Barbiellini had nothing of his own and that the brothers of the Servant of God had even his bridegroom's clothes made for him, as I heard from the very mouth of Mr. Checco, brother of the Servant of God. The Servant of God gave her daughter eighty thousand lire as dowry, and it was said that fifty thousand were the patrimony of the Servant of God and the other thirty thousand, I believe, the Servant of God drew from the rents accumulated over so many years.

In the first years, in Genoa, we Sisters of the Institute were lodged in the family villa of the Servant of God at Sampierdarena; this to say that the Servant of God had some personal property.

Proc. fol. 1199: It must be noted, then, that the son-in-law had a glib tongue and tried to show himself knowledgeable in business and construction, and when he spoke with us and with the Servant of God about the business done by us he criticized and said: «This I would have done in this and that other way»; so it was easy to believe that he would have succeeded in managing our affairs very well. He showed himself, moreover, very pious, approached the Sacraments, was a home-loving man, cut clothes, sewed them by machine, as I myself saw, so that the Sisters, not only out of respect for the Mother but also for his qualities, esteemed him highly at first. Thus he also succeeded in having some of our business carried out by a brother of his, by the name of Edoardo. He, however, took advantage of the trust of the Servant of God and of Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza to steal about ten thousand lire which at various times had been handed to him to send to the firm supplying our fabrics. He was discovered in January, before the death of the Servant of God, and I believe this was the cause of the collapse of her already ruined health.

And this was said among all of us.

§ 357
Dishonest expedients of the son-in-law toward the Servant of God.

Count Gaspare, seeing that the Servant of God was so attached to her daughter, sometimes resorted to rather dishonest expedients to wring money from his mother-in-law; as, for example, this: once he brought his daughter and the children to Piacenza, to our house, saying he wanted nothing more to do with them, and ran off.

When I was Superior in Florence, a Lady whom we had nursed in her illness left me at her death a deposit book at a bank. Wishing to send it to the Servant of God, I took advantage of the occasion when her son-in-law passed through Florence and gave it to him, asking him to cash it and bring the money to the Servant of God. I did not even look at the sum marked in the book, since I then held this son-in-law in the highest esteem. I received no notice from our mother of the arrival of the said book. I never dared speak to her about it, because of the great awe she inspired in me, and on the other hand it seemed to me I would be failing in respect for her by expressing to her the doubt of such a theft. But questioning the Sisters of the Secretariat afterward very casually, I was persuaded from their answers that she had received nothing, and more and more I was confirmed in my first idea, that the son-in-law had kept it for himself; an idea conceived because the Servant of God was in the habit of always thanking us after she had received money from us, and this time not only had she never thanked me, but she did not even speak to me of it.

Count Gaspare, when he wanted money from his mother-in-law, taught his children and his wife the art of succeeding in wresting it from her. Once, here in Rome (not many years before nineteen hundred), his daughter Carlotta presented herself suddenly to the Servant of God in her study, all upset, saying she had absolute need of money (I do not know what sum she asked). Then Carlotta's eldest son came in to complete the comedy and put the Servant of God ever more in a corner, and she, either because she had no money or because she did not wish to give it to them, refused. Suddenly Carlotta moved toward the window and made as if to throw herself down. One can well imagine how frightened the Servant of God was. I do not know whether she then yielded.

Of similar scenes to force the Servant of God to give money there occurred many. And the Servant of God gave them money; I recall, however, having often heard her say: «The money I give to my daughter and her family I can give, because it is not the Institute's money, but was given to me precisely for this purpose of helping my family».

Proc. fol. 1206v.: Concerning the relations of the Servant of God with her relatives I conclude by saying that she was most greatly tried by them.

§ 358
The son-in-law's accusations at the root of the Apostolic Visitation.

Ad 25: I recall only one Apostolic visitation made to the Institute, by the Benedictine Abbot Serafini, now Cardinal. I heard it said here in the house that this visitation came principally from the machinations of Count Gaspare Barbiellini, who had clashed greatly with the Servant of God because she had taken from him all administration and all interference in the affairs of the Institute.

It was said here in the house that among the accusations made by Barbiellini was this: that the approval, and a speedy one, of the rules had come principally from the sympathy between the Cardinal Protector, who was Prefect of the Bishops and Regulars, and Sr. Francesca. (He too had noticed this sympathy, because the Cardinal was often here, and he too.)

I know, and it was said here in the house, that Count Gaspare Barbiellini, irritated and jealous of the mutual benevolence between the Servant of God and his brother Federico, once went so far as to say that the Servant of God was a freemason, or something of the sort. What other precise accusations he made in petitions against the Servant of God, I do not know, but from the hatred that appears from what has been said so far, and from his exerting himself with great activity on the occasion of this Apostolic Visitation, going often to the Visitor and to the Cardinal Vicar, one can well conclude that he really had a part in procuring us this apostolic visitation, as was common opinion, and in presenting grave accusations against the Servant of God.

What was given to the Sisters was, according to Count Gaspare, always too much. He saw the meat we bought, and it was too much, and I suffered at hearing these observations made by the son-in-law of the Servant of God, while his children very often had a steak given to them in the kitchen (sometimes with the consent of the Servant of God), although afterward they took it home to eat. The supply of meat was already scanty in itself, and I suffered at having to have a steak taken out for those children; but I said nothing to the Servant of God, fearing to sadden her.

I vaguely recall that it was said that to the petitions of Count Gaspare others were joined from some Sister.

The appearance of the Visitor in Piacenza, where the Servant of God was, was a painful blow to her, and she bore this visitation with resignation. Every time the Visitor then came to the Servant of God, I saw that she always received him with respect. I recall that the Servant of God, in that time of the Apostolic Visitation, told the Sisters to set matters before the Visitor with sincerity and truth.

§ 360
Some religious criticized the relations of the Servant of God with her relatives.

Since a not inconsiderable number of Sisters looked unfavorably on the relatives' overly close contact with the Servant of God, I believe they were quite pleased that the occasion presented itself in which they could vent their feelings a little to a person of authority.

For example, the Superiors who came from elsewhere to this house to speak with the Servant of God and hand over to her the surplus of their administration often had to wait a long time before her study, because there was always one of her relatives in it. At last, when these had gone out, they could enter, but they felt very badly, because, as was natural, they wished to linger a little with the Servant of God, whereas she dispatched them with a certain haste, sending them back to their houses. The Servant of God, it is true, sometimes said to her little grandchildren: «Do not come today, let me get on, because today I have business with the Sisters»; but how could she send them away so often! They were children, and children are indiscreet: they liked being with their grandmother and so as soon as they were up they came to say good morning to her; they were sweet and pretty and we ourselves made a fuss of them. From one word to another ten minutes soon went by, and then they went on to the other Sisters of the Secretariat and then left. After dinner they generally came back once more to make the Servant of God lose another ten minutes. Then there was their mother, who could not be without seeing the Servant of God and, because of her difficulty in speaking, had to stay much longer, and the Servant of God, when she had more time, kept her longer and, when she had less, kept her less. It does not seem to me, however, that ordinarily she exceeded half an hour. I recall that the Servant of God sometimes said to her: «Come at such an hour, for then I am freer». Perhaps sometimes she may have kept her daughter much longer, because she was upset about some family matter, but this, if it happened, was very rare. Gaspare stayed only a short time, on business. The brother of the Servant of God, Federico, came more rarely, and only out of kindness. The brother Checco came often, but on business of the Institute, which he himself handled and for which he had to stay longer.

The Sisters, then, as I said before, who came from elsewhere and who would have wanted the Mother all to themselves, were badly impressed if they happened to land on some bad day because of the relatives' visits, and did not stop to distinguish whether Checco or Count Gaspare had come on business.

They saw that one succeeded another, and that they were relatives, and this grated on them.

§ 361
The Servant of God faithfully observed the commandments of God and the rules.

Ad 26: The Servant of God always and faithfully observed the Commandments of God, the Precepts of the Church and the obligations of her various states, and always had the rules of the Institute observed, inculcating them first by her examples and then by word; by her examples, because she, as long as she could, always observed them with the greatest exactness, even in the smallest things.

Ad 27: The Servant of God exercised the three Theological virtues, Faith, Hope and Charity, and also the Cardinal virtues, Prudence, Justice, Temperance and Fortitude; likewise she exercised the virtues of humility, obedience, poverty and chastity.

§ 362
Spirit of lively faith in the Servant of God.

Of Faith the Servant of God had much and lively, and I believe that, had the occasion presented itself, she would gladly have shed her blood for the faith. Most ardent was her desire that our faith be spread in souls, that children be instructed. For this her Sisters had to teach catechism wherever there were children to instruct; for this she sent the Sisters to Africa and to America. From the time she was a lay woman, frequenting the hospitals, while she served the sick she tried to instill holy faith into their hearts and to instruct them. When she was afterward a Religious, she did the same with the sick in their homes and wanted us Sisters at the bedside of the sick, whether in homes or in hospitals, to do likewise. She prayed for unbelievers and sinners and prescribed for us some prayers that we still recite. When Sisters were to leave for Africa and America, she gave them exhortations, that they might take the most diligent care of the poor unbelievers. Seeing the abundant fruits drawn from our missions in Africa, those missions became her favorites. I too heard her show her gratitude and thank God for having made her be born in the Catholic Religion.

§ 363
Veneration of the Holy Father. Zeal for the house of God.

Proc. fol. 1232: The Servant of God paid all veneration to the Supreme Pontiff, not only in words but also in deeds.

For Pius IX she then had a special reverence and veneration. Every time her Sisters came to Rome, she wanted them to visit Pius IX, and to me, who was Superior of this house, she said: «Take them to the Holy Father», so that one year I saw him eight times. It must be noted that, Mgr. Negrotto, a Genoese, being then Secret Chamberlain in Attendance, it was enough that we present ourselves to him to be then received at once by the Holy Father. Once Pius IX gave the Servant of God some most beautiful pears, and she, out of veneration, did not wish to eat them, but had them put in spirits, where for so many years they were preserved, and I do not know how they ended.

Every time the Servant of God presented herself to Pius IX, he made much of her.

With Pope Leo XIII the visits were naturally a little rarer, indeed very rare, he not receiving so easily; but she paid equal homage to him, and showed it by speaking of the Pope with us, exhorting us to submission and veneration toward the Pope.

The Servant of God was solicitous for the Churches and Chapels of our Institute, and watched also over the cleanliness of the Churches and Chapels where she was and through which she passed.

§ 364
Firm hope and detachment from the goods of the earth.

The Servant of God without doubt exercised the virtue of Hope, which she showed in her discourses, which made one see her hope of going to Paradise through the merits of Jesus Christ. She was not at all attached to the goods of this earth, as was shown in the exercise of rigorous poverty. She had recourse to prayer in her difficulties and anguish, and not only did she pray herself, but she made the Novices and Sisters pray too, not only to overcome difficulties but also to obtain other graces.

With her word she still infused Hope into the Sisters. «Hope in God», she said to us; and when some Superior of a poor house complained of straitened circumstances, she answered: «Observe the rule, and Providence will not fail you». She sought to infuse the virtue of Hope not only into the Sisters but also into all the afflicted and tried who had recourse to her. And how much the Servant of the Lord hoped for all from God is made plain by the following fact.

I, with another Sister, had nursed Canon Maffi, who was ill, of Piacenza. In the end, although at first I refused out of respect for our ancient rule, he wished to give me an envelope containing money in gratitude. I was persuaded that I would be very well received by the Servant of God by bringing her home a little money, because our Institute was in its beginnings and had great need of it, and therefore as soon as I arrived home, without even taking off the large veil, I presented myself with the envelope to the Servant of God; but she, without even looking at the sum the envelope contained, gave me a good reprimand for having failed the rule and, handing the envelope back to me, said: «Go, take the envelope back to the canon at once».

The Servant of God exercised also the virtue of charity toward God and toward neighbor.

§ 365
Fervent love of God.

She avoided venial sins and was most observant of every rule, as I have already said in another session; and she saw to it that others too kept far from sin and did good works instead.

When she heard coarse words or blasphemies, or some offense against God was reported to her, «Oh God, oh God», she would say, and with her right thumb she signed herself on the forehead, and showed sorrow. She exhorted Sisters and outsiders to the love of God, and her words were truly penetrating. When she came out of Church, the Servant of God was all aglow in the face, and seemed a Seraph of love.

§ 366
Spiritual and temporal charity toward neighbor.

When and as she could, she practiced the spiritual and corporal works of mercy. She consoled the afflicted, and her words were effective. It happened to me too to present myself to her for some affliction, and I went away wholly consoled.

While on the one hand the Servant of God knew how to correct even severely, on the other she showed no aversion toward anyone, not even toward those persons who had offended her.

She helped the poor, handed out bread to them on Saturday, as is still done today in this House and in Piacenza; she also handed out soup, and I have heard it said that for a certain very sad time she handed it out every day, distributing it personally herself. In this house the custom of the Servant of God is still followed of handing out also pasta on certain solemnities, such as Easter, Christmas, St. Anne. She made little bodices, little shirts, etc. for poor children.

Toward the sick her charity is shown by the purpose of her Institute; and to the poor among them, besides going or sending to assist them, she also sent broth, little pasta, etc.

Since the principal purpose of the Institute is to assist the sick, she had for us nursing Sisters a special predilection in comparison with our sister Teachers.

Proc. fol. 1241: The said three Theological virtues the Servant of God exercised in an extraordinary degree, and as a true Saint, as I have read in some lives of Saints. So it seems to me I must say, for the truth.

§ 367
She practiced prudence in a notable manner.
§ 368
She prayed, had others pray, and took counsel in important matters.

As to the Cardinal virtues, to begin with Prudence, I say that of this virtue the Servant of God possessed a great deal. We turned with great trust to the Servant of God in everything of ours. We were above all sure that whatever we confided to her remained with her. Then, although she corrected us even severely, she knew how to do so in such a way that we never ceased to see in her our true Mother, and the trust we had did not diminish in the least. Indeed, allow me a comparison: although the late Mother Carrega is unforgettable for us for her maternal kindness, and was all heart for us, I nonetheless remember well that during the government of the late Mother Carrega I missed the trust I had in turning to the Servant of God, who had inspired more of it in me than Carrega.

When she had something important in hand, she not only prayed and had the Sisters pray, but also asked counsel of the Cardinal Protector and of her Assistants. We Assistants, however, looked to our Mother, for whom we had the greatest veneration. There was in her an I-know-not-what of the extraordinary, by which we always adhered to what she proposed to us. As far as I know, I must say that the Servant of God always governed the Institute with prudence, that she never proceeded lightly in her decisions. She was a woman in whom holiness was truly seen.

I always noticed her prudence also in the reprimands she gave us, in which, as I said, she was severe indeed, but had also an I-know-not-what that compelled one to submit to her. When she then saw the Sister repentant, she treated her with gentleness and encouraged her.

§ 369
She practiced justice in an evangelical way.

As to Justice, I must say that the Servant of God not only gave to each his due, but also showed herself grateful to those who did her or the Institute some favor. She prayed and had others pray for Benefactors, and prescribed it for us in our rules. For the posts and offices of the Institute she did not let herself be guided by sympathies or secondary ends, but disposed according to aptitudes, qualities and merits.

§ 370
She was strong and infused Christian fortitude into others.

She was a truly strong woman, and declared that the day on which she had nothing to suffer seemed lost to her, and she desired to carry the cross.

To us Sisters she then gave courage with energetic words, besides her example. She never lost heart under the cross, and was wont to say: «To suffer is for me to rejoice».

The Servant of God was of a lively and ardent character, but one saw very well that she was restraining herself from the first years that I knew her. And I noticed in this virtue a continual crescendo.

§ 371
Spirit of penance and mortification.

I do not remember ever having seen her, even for a moment, idle, not even during recreation; and in this time she worked, as I said yesterday, for the poor. She was a tireless worker. The Servant of God was not only temperate, but was also penitent. I do not know when she began to eat meatless food; it is certain that as a Religious she never ate meat. In the morning she took coffee alone, without bread and without sugar, in a small cup. In the last years, however, to the black coffee she added a little chocolate, but this happened rarely. At noon she ate a Genoese minestrone, a little fish, sometimes eggs and a mixed salad. The Secretary saw to it that good fish was served to her, and was grieved to tears when she saw that the Mother did not eat the things procured by her.

Sometimes her brothers from Genoa sent her fresh fish, or, coming to Rome, brought it to her (this naturally could happen three or four times a year); but she, faced with these attentions, felt ill at ease and said: «But potatoes are enough for me»; and these she truly ate willingly.

§ 372
Spirit of evangelical poverty.

She was poor in her clothing, but clean. She herself put stitches in her threadbare habit, and the Secretary, the late Mother Carrega, who could not bear to see her Mother in clothes that were too old and worn, replaced them with new ones. This, however, brought her scoldings from the Servant of God, when she noticed.

Her linen was the common kind of the other Sisters. Her room was poor; there were no bedside tables. Only two work tables and four chairs. If I am not mistaken, from 1887 there was in winter a carpet in her room here in this house, which was placed there because the building was recent and damp. Her room in Piacenza, however, had truly no comfort at all. We entered it only after she was dead, and it is frightening. The present Bishop of Piacenza, when he saw that room, was moved to tears. There is in that room a great cross, formed of two heavy beams, which I do not know how the Servant of God was able to drag up there.

§ 373
She practiced humility in an uncommon degree.

Proc. fol. 1252v.: The Servant of God was distinguished also for humility. She did not like good works to be made public, but wished that the Institute grow in humility and hiddenness. Of herself I never heard that she spoke, and even when something turned out well for her, she attributed everything to God, not only inwardly but also in the conversations she had with us. And in her humble speech one saw no ostentation, but sincerity and naturalness. She always said she was nothing but a poor sinner. And when she saw some fine result in the Institute, she said to us: «Oh! how good the Lord is to us!».

§ 374
Obedient and very deferential toward superiors.

As to obedience, besides what I have said of her submission to the Ecclesiastical Superiors, I must say that in a particular way she was submissive to the Cardinal Protector. She wanted the Sisters who came to Rome from afar or left it to present themselves to the Cardinal Protector. I believe she was most deferential to all those whose counsel she asked, because they showed that they continued always to esteem her. I recall among her counselors Fr. Vincenzo d'Alatri, Capuchin, to whom she confessed in the last three years, Cardinal di Belmonte, Fr. Bresciani, Redemptorist, and Fr. Bernardino da Portogruaro.

I recall that once, finding herself perplexed about the acceptance of a house, she listened to me, who urged her to accept it.

§ 375
She loved and practiced chastity joyfully.

Proc. fol. 1258v.: The Servant of God was Chastity in person. It was enough to look at her to have the impression of her purity. This already says enough about her bearing, both as to the eyes and as to the rest. I never heard that she spoke of her marriage. She did not want the Sisters to give their hand to lay people, and she set the example. She was vigilant and did not allow postcards not sufficiently modest to reach the Sisters, and if they arrived, she had them burned. We do the same now, following her example.

I recall that when I was in Genoa I had learned an expression whose import I did not know, and do not know even now. The Servant of God, hearing it, told me not to say it any more. Since we had to be in Hospitals and exposed to so many dangers, the Servant of God herself said to us: «We must keep a very reserved bearing and never remain alone». This was her principal point in her exhortations. She recommended to the teachers that they not form particular friendships with the children; that they be on their guard with school inspectors, and with them too never remain alone.

As far as I know, the Servant of God, in the Theological virtues as in the Cardinal, as also in all the other virtues of which I have spoken, persevered always until death. And in my judgment she always progressed in the exercise of those same virtues.

§ 376
She exercised all the virtues to a heroic degree.

Ad 28: I have already spoken of the heroism of the Theological virtues. As to the Cardinal and others, I believe in conscience I can affirm the same of the others, that is, that she exercised all of them to a heroic degree, that is, as a Saint of the altar: she exercised them in a way that had become natural to her, without effort, with ease.

p. 223

§ 377
Conditioned by her daughter's state in relations with relatives.

As to her relations with her relatives, her conduct depended not on her, but on the conditions of her daughter and of her other relatives; and therefore I do not feel in any way able to make a reproach of it to her. And we Sisters would have felt neither the wish nor the courage to oppose the visits of her relatives, whom we too loved very much, and especially the little grandchildren and the deaf-mute daughter.
